#6568. Vogue’s Best Dressed People of 2026

Our goal was 50—just 50!—of the best-dressed people of the year, a list to commemorate the unforgettable fashion moments of a very topsy-turvy 2026. Sounds easy…but, well, list-making never is. There were athletes who turned game days into runways, actors who owned the red carpet and the sidewalk, and method-dressing movie stars who artfully ignored the meaning of the word cut.

We wanted them all, plus some highly fashionable characters from unexpected fields and walks of life, and we wanted couples, which we insisted should be counted as singletons (a technicality!). We struggled and horse-traded and voted and arrived finally at…55! (The same number as last year.) Here is the fruit of our labor: an unranked, diligently categorized, highly subjective list of Vogue’s best dressed of 2026. And it all begins with our cover star, a selection that was the result of a rather heated debate. Enjoy!

Written by: Christian Allaire, Margaux Anbouba, Taylor Antrim, Max Berlinger, Laird Borrelli-Persson, Anna Cafolla, Liam Hess, Alexandra Hildreth, Hannah Jackson, Joan Kennedy, Irene Kim, Anna Grace Lee, Nicole Phelps, Madeleine Schulz, and Emma Specter.

STORRIE TIME Conner Storrie brings the Ken-ergy in a miniaturized version of his Gucci Best Dressed cover look. Coach watch pendant.

Why 2026 was his year: Playing brooding Russian hockey player Ilya Rozanov in the gay romance Heated Rivalry—in various states of deshabille—launched this 26-year-old Hollywood hopeful waiting tables in Los Angeles to cultural supernova. His last 12 months have seen a kind of fashion miracle: Storrie is now better known for what he wears than what he doesn’t. Click here for his cover-story conversation with Chloe Malle—which ranged from Storrie’s punk roots to his adoration of Parker Posey, his side hustle in “provocateur” photography, and more.

Friends, lovers, collaborators—occasionally all at once.

Why 2026 was their year: Him: Train Daddy in The Gilded Age; Her: Wicked stepmother in Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story (and more).

Their couple style, in essence: Hudson Valley cabincore meets Tom Ford heat.

Kravitz wears The Row. Styles wears The Row and Adidas.

Their year in fashion: Excellent outerwear, statement headgear, rave-ready sunglasses, plenty of The Row.

Their couple style, in essence: Kiss all the time. Dress alike, more than occasionally.

From left: Imhof wears Balenciaga, Teuscher wears Rodarte; both wear Valentino.

Why 2026 was their year: Teuscher traded Lincoln Center for Hong Kong to star in her partner Imhof’s queer, Shakespearean House of Swans.

Their couple style, in essence: Berghain Romeo and Juliet.

Why 2026 was their year: Barone released comedy special Galaxy Brain; Skinner got to work on Overcompensating season 2. Together: their riotous podcast, Ride, and Halloween domination.

Their couple style, in essence: Newport Beach heartthrobs, if they canvassed for Zohran.

Left: Both in Dior. Right: Arquette wears Circus of Magdela; Lean wears Giorgio Armani.

Why 2026 was their year: Lean bringing down the house at the VMAs, while writing duets with Arquette; the couple hard-launching at Dior Men’s spring 2027 show.

Their couple style, in essence: Shades of blue (or bleu).

Left: Rosalía in Stella McCartney. Right: Bahia wears Saint Laurent; Rosalía wears Vivienne Westwood.

Their year in fashion: Contrasting-yet-coordinated masc-for-femme dressing, conjuring early days Justin and Hailey.

Why we can’t get enough: Two words: tooth necklace.

He said; she said: MGK to Vogue: “I started kind of respecting my upkeep, and I’ve watched things open up.” Johnson to Vogue: “[Musicians] like me, I don’t know what to say.”

Their couple style, in essence: Hoodies, diamonds, beanies, grommets, lace, leather, fangs. Misery business.

LIFE IN PLASTIC, IT’S FANTASTIC! Master of the step-and-repeat, Kendall Jenner set the gold standard for polka-dots in her Valentino Academy Gala dress.

The category is: great gowns, beautiful gowns.

Jenner wears Armani; Alexander Calder earrings.

Her year in fashion: Winged Victory at the Met, snagging ultra-rare Calder earrings for her first Lido, spreading the gospel of The Row, and perfecting polka dots at the Academy Gala.

Why we can’t get enough: She wears clothes like it’s her job.

Why 2026 was her year: Rose, Fatherland, and Project Hail Mary! (And, ahem, Digger.)

Highlight reel: Matières Fécales’ riff on the bar suit; Chanel’s riff on the hedgehog.

Her year in fashion: Dior standouts (acid green Poiret punk and impressionistic water lilies, specifically), plus an Issey Miyake breastplate, Marc Jacobs sequins, and Lii color blocking.

Best look of 2026: That star-spangled scarlet High Sport halter dress with a swishy fringed hem for the London premiere of Toy Story 5—a clever, playful wink to the film’s universe that still felt fashion.

Mulligan wears (from left): Colleen Allen; Dries Van Noten; The Row; Celine.

Why 2026 was her year: Lending her voice to Wildwood, scoring an Emmy nom for Beef season 2, getting a CBE from the King (she wore The Row).

Best look: That triptych of pixelated floral brocades from Julian Klausner’s fall 2026 Dries Van Noten collection. Bonus points for the pockets in the top!

Why this was her year: An awards-season run for Hamnet; an ultra-chic stint on the jury at Cannes.

Best look of 2026: Schiaparelli’s spiky “Isabella Blowfish” dress was a creepy-cheeky wow on the runway—and doubly satisfying on the Croisette.

A DOLL’S HOUSE Who says you can only wear your Met Gala dress once? Back in her Barbie Dreamhouse closet, Paloma Elsesser plays dress-up in her bespoke Bureau of Imagination gown.

They’re wearing your favorite brand—you just don’t know it yet.

Elsesser wears (from left): Junya Watanabe; Comme des Garçons, Phoebe Philo shoes, Chanel bag; Goyagoma.

Why 2026 was her year: When she wasn’t on the hunt for her next vintage deep cut? Hitting the runway for Ferragamo and Junya Watanabe and debuting Francesco Risso’s Bureau of Imagination at the Met.

She’ll get bragging rights for: The Bureau of Imagination gown—patchworked, painted, and embellished by “a squadron of people.” A true one-of-a-kind.

Thompson wears Giovanna Flores; Kallmeyer.

Why 2026 was her year: A Golden Globes nomination for Hedda; the runaway thriller His & Hers; and her Broadway debut in Fear of 13 alongside Adrien Brody.

She’ll get bragging rights for: Her support of all things indie is as evident in her work as in her wardrobe: just take the enviably cool Giovanna Flores patchwork dress she wore on a sweltering day in New York.

Peak wears (from left): Lii; Diotima; Torishéju.

Why 2026 was her year: She drummed up Hunger Games hype, toggling her looks between indie darlings and bona fide fashion-girl pulls.

She’ll get bragging rights for wearing: A scrunched-up black top and red cut-out leather skirt from London-based Torishéju; the standout textured Diotima dress from this season; and New York favorite Liii.

She’ll get bragging rights for wearing: A custom dress from Polimoda fashion school graduate Elias Matso, made entirely from steel boning and beads in a process that took over 300 hours.

Her year in fashion: Ditching goth—at least until Wednesday season 3.

OUT OF THE BOX On the lively streets of New York City, Sarah Pidgeon does her best CBK in a leopard-print Adam Lippes coat. Susan Alexandra pigeon charm.

Why 2026 was her year: She introduced a new generation to Carolyn Bessette-Kennedy—and her Yohji Yamamoto-filled closet—in Love Story.

Give her an Oscar for this look: The lacy aqua blue slip dress she wore to the Chanel Pre-Oscars party married CBK-ish ’90s minimalism with present-day Blazy-mania.

Why 2026 was her year: The Drama! Spider-Man! The Odyssey! Dune! Oh, and she found time to marry Tom Holland, too.

Give her an Oscar for this look: The white strapless Matières Fécales gown with matching feathered wings while promoting The Odyssey was pure Athena realness.

Edgar-Jones wears (from left): Miu Miu; Andreas Kronthaler for Vivienne Westwood; Rodarte.

Why 2026 was her year: The 18th-century-inspired Sense and Sensibility press tour, featuring a dreamy blush Galliano jacket worn with jeans; sexed-up pantaloon sets from Dries Van Noten and Colleen Allen; and lots and lots of Stella McCartney-era Chloé.

Up next: Going toe-to-toe with Michelle Williams in A Place in Hell and bringing another book club favorite to the big screen in Tomorrow, and Tomorrow, and Tomorrow.

Robbie wears Schiaparelli; Dilara Findikoglu.

Why we can’t get enough: Schiaparelli couture with Elizabeth Taylor’s legendary Taj Mahal diamonds one day, cutoff jorts the next.

Up Next: How will she method-dress for Untitled Ocean’s Eleven Prequel?

Fanning wears (from left): Robert Wun; Givenchy by Sarah Burton; Evan Clayton.

Why 2026 was her year: Earned her first Oscar nomination for Sentimental Value, delivered Margot’s Got Money Troubles, and dressed in her Capitol best for The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.

Her style, in essence: Anything can be a hat!

OFF THE SHELF Olivia Rodrigo, here in vintage Rudi Gernreich, brought major flower power with her inaugural Daisy Chain Fields festival. Susan Alexandra flower and mushroom charms.

Pop stars or politicians—they’re all headliners to us.

Why 2026 was her year: It was a legacy-defining one between Rodrigo’s best album yet (hello, seven Grammy nominations) and her inaugural Daisy Chain Fields music festival, which raised $20 million to support nonprofits for women and girls.

Her year in fashion: She joined a long line of badasses who’ve subverted the babydoll dress—Kathleen Hanna and Courtney Love come to mind.

Why we can’t get enough: From this summer’s ribbon-cutting at the Barack Obama Presidential Center in Thom Browne to attending the U.S. Open in red, white, and blue Chanel, she makes patriotism look chic.

The look that deserved a push notification: The Acne Studios skirt custom-printed with a photo of her late mother Marian Robinson, a gesture that brought the former president—and the rest of us—to tears.

Dion wears (from left): Tom Ford; Dior; Chanel; Chanel.

Why 2026 was their year: A triumphant return to the stage following her stiff person syndrome diagnosis meant 16 sold-out shows at Paris’s Plénitude Arena, plus daily pap walks outside of Le Royal Monceau.

The look that deserved a push notification: The custom Chanel sweetheart-neckline gown that took 1,380 hours to make—a recreation of her 1997 Oscars dress. Our hearts will go on!

Why 2026 was her year: Wrestling with mortality on Lost Weekend; stealing scenes in Primetime.

The look that deserved a push notification: In Venice, a lesson in indie-darling dressing: Gucci skirt suit, below-the-knee tattoo, visible leg hair.

Why 2026 was her year: The Minnesota senator-to-be’s midterm victory made her the first-ever Indigenous woman elected to the United States Senate.

The look that deserved a push notification: Victory called for a sleek burgundy suit and a traditional pair of dentalium shell earrings by Yurok artist Jessica Mendez.

TINY FURNITURE Just like Mary, Cole Escola is the picture-perfect homemaker in the Christopher John Rogers jumpsuit they wore to the Tonys. Movado watch. Jennifer Behr earrings.

Imitation may be the sincerest form of flattery, but there’s no replicating one-of-one style.

Escola wears (from left): Chanel; Eckhaus Latta; vintage Eve Stillman.

Why 2026 was their year: Oh, Mary! went on the road, and Escola’s Miss Piggy became the in-the-works screenplay we didn’t know we needed.

Highlight reel: Coco cosplay at Chanel couture; an “ibuprofen”-pink Christopher John Rogers jumpsuit at the Tonys; an Eckhaus Latta deep cut at the CFDA Awards.

Why 2026 was her year: Who else could collect their Golden Globe in a bejeweled Schiaparelli whale tail?

Her best look: The trompe l’oeil Thom Browne at the SAG Awards, with her daughter Rue Rose on hand to adjust her train. As Taylor put it: “A very expensive stylist.”

Why 2026 was his year: A longtime Comme des Garçons acolyte, Sedaris promoted his latest book, The Land and Its People, in layers of deconstructed tailoring, voluminous skirts, and oddball shoes.

Why we can’t get enough: Dressed in a diaphanous layered ensemble for Late Night With Seth Meyers, he quipped, “I think of this as a sports skirt.”

Ellis Ross wears (from left): Prada; Balenciaga; Dries Van Noten.

Why this was her year: A Broadway debut in Every Brilliant Thing, an expanding Pattern Beauty lineup, a daytime Emmy for her show, Solo Traveling—and she found time to start styling herself.

Best look of 2026: That marigold Balenciaga at the 2026 Academy Museum Gala; beautifully textured, quintessentially her (with a dash of Law Roach).

Why we can’t get enough: What was the American Hagwon author’s first fashion flex when fiction started paying the bills? Early days Thom Browne. “I bought one of Thom’s first sweaters,” Lee told Vogue.

Best look of 2026: Her go-to matching pinstriped Comme des Garçons blazer and dress for large speaking events. Who said a uniform can’t have style?

Hill wears (from left): Bottega Veneta; Saint Laurent; Balenciaga.

Why 2026 was her year: Became a BET Living Legend in voluminous, ruffled Saint Laurent with wrap-around sunglasses; reunited with Wyclef to celebrate the 30th anniversary of The Score; sat front row at Balenciaga spring 2027 as “Ready or Not” blared.

Her style in essence: Can’t take my eyes off you.

PAPER DOLL Audrey Nuna puts a bow on 2026 in the Thom Browne cape she wore to the Golden Globes.

You’ll never again have to ask, “Wait, where do I know them from?”

Where you know her from: If you don’t know her face, odds are you’ve heard her sing: Nuna lent her voice to Mira in the Oscar- and Grammy-winning KPop Demon Hunters.

Best outfit of 2026: The cocoon-like black cape dress embellished with bows from Thom Browne—one of her more understated looks, if you can believe it.

You’ve heard them: Honking on their Getting Killed tour, SNL, or frontman Cameron Winter’s Carnegie Hall live album.

Their year in fashion: Well-worn band tees, threadbare tank tops, bug-eyed sunglasses, and dresses over jeans are par for the course. Their too-cool-for-school style is just that: too cool.

Why you should know her: The singer was marked safe from one-hit-wonderdom with her third album, Blue Island.

Best outfit of 2026: The eccentric, richly embellished Space Age Rabanne dress she wore to the Grammys was totally out of this world.

Where you know her from: Apple TV’s Shrinking and Kane Parsons’s instant horror classic Backrooms.

Best outfit of 2026: The peachy fall 2011 Prada minidress with rounded sleeves, sharp front pleats, and a belted drop waist that she wore during the Toronto International Film Festival. If Miuccia hasn’t already come calling…she should.

Why you should know her: The actor—and niece of fashion designer Anna Sui—proved good taste is genetic while making the rounds for I Want Your Sex and The Studio.

Best outfit of 2026: At Sundance, she plumbed the family archives, settling on a funky, faux fur-trimmed slip dress and matching bonnet. She got it from her auntie!

Great on the red carpet; even better on a morning-after coffee run.

Lawrence wears (from left): Dior jacket, Completedworks earrings; The Row polo, Siedrés pants, Tory Burch necklace, The Row loafers; Junk Food T-shirt, Dries Van Noten skirt, Ancient Greek slippers, Hermès bag.

Her year in fashion: Vintage graphic tees; flowing trousers; boho scarves; slip-on Vans; oversized sunglasses; pendant necklaces; statement bags of the highest order.

Her style, in essence: Skate park chaperone.

Jacobson wears (from left): Khaite; Dilara Findikoglu; Mel Usine; Conner Ives.

Why we can’t get enough: The theatricality we want from a Yale Drama grad: high collars, slashed abs, daring necklines, sleek layering.

On the clock: Her 2026 Met Gala look—as a Joan of Arc-esque figure in a coin-and-pin-adorned armored bodysuit by Dilara Findikoglu. Biopic when?

Edebiri wears (from left): Conner Ives; Giovanna Flores; vintage tee, Still Kelly pants, Chanel bag.

Why this was her year: Post-Bear, trying new things with her career (Broadway; Woolf), and her fashion (Giovanna Flores patchwork dress; Chanel tail feathers).

Best look of 2026: She showed the boys how it’s done in a slick Conner Ives suit.

Schafer wears (from left): Prada; Gimaguas dress; Celine.

Best off-duty look of 2026: The silky purple backward button-up over a tomato-red Gimaguas minidress she wore down the Chateau Marmont driveway.

Her style, in essence: Up for anything, from Gustav Klimt’s Mäda Primavesi to dystopian fembot.

Abrams wears (from left): Balenciaga by Nicolas Ghesquière top, Hamish Olrik pants, Chanel shoes; Colleen Allen; vintage tee from Moth Food, Chanel pants, shoes, and bag.

Best off-duty look of 2026: The sporty, vintage-looking “Vote” baseball tee paired with high-waisted wool trousers and Chanel’s signature cap-toe shoes: effortless, elegant, utterly cool.

Her style, in essence: West LA girl on London sabbatical.

MVPs and benchwarmers alike stole the show with their ’fits this year.

Osaka wears Miss Claire Sullivan; Hana Yagi.

Why 2026 was her year: The four-time Grand Slam champ reached her first-ever Wimbledon quarterfinal and went all-in on her fashion, on and off the court.

Her slam-dunk look: Acing Wimbledon whites in a Hana Yagi walkout look inspired by traditional Japanese ceremonial attire.

Clarkson wears (from left): Abercrombie & Fitch; vintage T-shirt, Louis Vuitton scarf, Hat Club hat; Chrome Hearts jacket, Saint Laurent pants.

His slam-dunk look: A fitted black Rick Owens long-sleeve and pants amidst the Paris heatwave. He ditched the shirt post-show—not that we’re complaining.

Why 2026 was his year: A ruptured Achilles and dashed World Cup dreams didn’t keep the French footballer from Wimbledon or the Balenciaga front row.

His slam-dunk look: A Miu Miu Canadian tuxedo, vested for maximum bicep-baring.

They are not like other guys, in that you’ll never catch them in a snoozy black tux.

O’Connor wears (from left): Lemaire; vintage jacket, Adidas track pants; Hermès.

Best look of 2026: The all-black Hermès leather shirt-and-trousers ensemble that gagged the internet.

Why we can’t get enough: The swerve from tweedy London boy to louche fashion lad. We always knew he had it in him.

#6567. I Prepared for This A.I. Chaos Moment for Over a Year. Here Is What I’ve Learned.

If your group chats look anything like mine, you’ve spent some of the past week wondering whether something big was unfolding. As air traffic halted, Microsoft 365 went down, and Chase Bank and dozens of important websites, including the NSA’s internal classified network, experienced an array of outages, it started to seem plausible that stuff the artificial intelligence whistleblowers have been warning us about (swarms of rogue agents, AI-powered cyber attacks) was happening already. How worried should we be about the AI apocalypse? On the one hand, Claude doesn’t even have hands, LOL. On the other hand, in a battle between AI and the creaky digital infrastructure that underlays all aspects of modern life, it wouldn’t require a superintelligence to launch the final spinning wheel of death.

I consider myself a normie centrist—not too prone to conspiracy theories. During Covid, I stocked up on toilet paper and some bags of beans and rice (still unopened on my shelves) and shattered my collarbone mountain biking when we were all supposed to be hunkered down indoors during lockdown. But I also listen to a lot of podcasts. Enough that my friends and partner have told me that a digital detox might improve my mental health and, by extension, theirs. And, lately, the podcasts have sent me plunging into a Mach tuck of terminal anxiety.

The Pod Save the World boys are joking about building their stores of beef jerky. “Should I be, like, stocking up my bunker now?” Kevin Roose, cohost of Machine Gods asked his guest Ben Buchanan, the first White House Special Advisor for AI. There’s an obligatory chuckle that talking heads do now when discussing the AI apocalypse in front of an audience. “A month ago we were talking about normal things, ha ha,” Steve Eisman, finance guru of The Big Short fame, said on his podcast on October 12, “And now we’re talking about the end of the world.” But it’s hard to casually segue from the end of the world to Anthropic’s IPO and not sound like a crank. So that laugh leaks out, and maybe it’s just a joke?

But count me as a genuine worrier. This week I withdrew enough cash in hundreds from a Bank of America branch that the teller started to interview me. “Doing some home renovations? Making a big purchase?” he asked.

“No, I’m worried as shit about AI, and in case you haven’t noticed it, banks aren’t doing so well right now,” I replied. In line with me were several people who couldn’t pay their credit card bills online because the payment portal had gone down.

We’ve been hearing about the existential risk of AI for a while now. I got into it last year by reading Eliezer Yudkowsky and Nate Soares’s book, If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies, after hearing Yudkowsky interviewed on Ezra Klein’s podcast. This is a terrible book for someone who’s prone to worry because it relies on nontechnical metaphors and colorful analogies. Superintelligence is like a chessmaster. You don’t need to know the moves it’ll make to be certain it wins. True! Superintelligence, they say, will be like a new species that is so much smarter than us that, if it doesn’t really really truly love us more than our own mothers and want to keep us alive, it will kill us all. The same way we crush ants when we build skyscrapers. There’s no malice toward us. We just got in the way.

Over the past year I—casually, at first—started amassing supplies. My adventure hobbies give me an excuse. I need this 6,500-watt generator for elk-hunting camp. These 400-watt EcoFlow solar panels power a giant battery so I can bring my Starlink Mini on camping trips. I listen to history podcasts, and these offer more inspiration. There was a recent NPR one about the Carrington solar flare of 1859, which fried telegraph wires across the country. An event like that, in 2026, might knock out the grid for months. Another good reason to be prepared. I tell my partner that it’s normal for us to keep 500 pounds of dry goods in the cupboards at all times. Everyone does this. We already have three 3,000-gallon cisterns. We live in the desert; they came with the house. Did we need another 400-gallon one? It was just laying in the neighbors’ yard. Why wouldn’t I hook that up to the gutters?

I spent a lot of the summer using AI to program an app for backcountry adventurers, so I knew firsthand it was already smarter than me. The doomsday chatter started to meet me where I was around the time of the Hugging Face incident in July. Then Jacob Coxon quit Anthropic in September so he could tweet that Anthropic and OpenAI are “gambling with our lives.” On November 5, independent evaluator METR found that Anthropic’s AI was already helping build its own successors—roughly doubling the company’s pace of progress and shifting expert predictions for major disruptions closer to the present. At the Hinton Lectures, in Toronto, OpenAI board member Paul Christiano calmly told the audience, “I think for most people in this room, the most likely reason they will die is because of an AI accident.”

Friends who are less prone to apocalyptic thinking than I am tend to point out that the people ringing the alarm about AI never spell out exactly which chess moves AI uses to kill us. But the week after the lecture, there was Christiano on another one of my podcasts, Dwarkesh Patel’s show, explaining one such scenario.

First, rogue AI agents create mischief of one kind or another. Then, the Trump administration tells Americans that the only way to wrest power back from the bots is to have the military take control of all data centers, the AI companies, and shut down the internet. This feels like an authoritarian power grab. It sets up civil unrest against the backdrop of a heavily lopsided information war, in which it’s almost impossible to tell which side anyone is on. Have the bots compromised the humans? Are the humans using the bots? Judging by how well everyone agreed on the facts around things like Covid and the 2020 election, our expectations should be low for how we’d perform as a society. Which brings us to the question of guns.

I don’t think of myself as really owning any guns at all. I believe that the fastest way to get shot is to start getting into gunfights. I personally know exactly zero civilians who have solved a problem with a firearm, but I know many who have made problems, including my own mother.

About 15 years ago, she called me one day from the dog park sounding flustered. She liked to shop for musical instruments and power tools at ShopGoodwill.com, and lately the boxes had gone missing from her porch in Spokane, Washington. “You’re not going to set a trap, are you?” I asked. Our minds worked the same way.

“Well, I already did,” she said. And that was why she was hiding from the police in the dog park.

She’d left a decoy package on the porch. A woman came to grab it, and my mother burst through the door two-handing her Sig Sauer the way she’d been trained at the Federal Law Enforcement Training Center in Glynco, Georgia, when she was starting her encore career as a CBP officer after 9/11. The woman claimed to be returning the package, not stealing it. A standoff ensued. My mom eventually backed down and the lady called the cops. My mom never responded to the phone calls from the police, and the whole thing just went away.

So when it comes to guns, I think, what am I actually going to use this for? To fend off hungry neighbors? To join a well-regulated militia and maybe become a dystopian warlord? Maybe it’s as simple as guns are addictive and it’s fun to ring the steel at 500 yards. I’ve put together a couple of rifles out of parts—an MDT chassis here, a Howa barreled action there—for other members of the family to hunt with, but I only do archery. And shotguns don’t really count as guns, especially when they’re the fancy break-action models with florid engravings of bygone scenes afield. “How many guns are in this house?” my partner wants to know. She really wanted to pin me down. “Counting the unmounted lower receiver stashed in the floorboards in the attic? Eight.”

My name is Grayson, and I have somehow become a prepper. It has not made me better off. It has made me poorer, and it has put me into contact with seedier elements of the general populace. I have what psychologists call a bias toward action, when the best thing to do is probably nothing at all. And I listen to too many podcasts.

One of them, from a year ago, really stuck with me. It was an episode of the financial podcast Prof G Markets. On it, I heard Aswath Damodaran, the NYU Stern valuation professor, tell the show’s wunderkind British cohost, Ed Elson, what he was doing with his money. “There’s no place to hide in stocks,” Damodaran said. “For the first time ever, I am looking at parking my money into one, cash, and two, collectibles or physical assets.” That a guy as sober as Damodaran was talking up baseball cards and physical gold coins was shocking.

It was less shocking when, this week, Barstool Sports personality Daniel “Big Cat” Katz posted screenshots purporting to show internal discussions with Dave Portnoy and Jersey Jerry about warning staff to “buy all the gold and silver u can.” I have a quick word of warning for anyone considering following Jersey Jerry’s advice.

Back in October, I asked Claude (I know, it’s ironic) for a recommendation on a reputable place to buy gold coins. It gave me a Texas-based website that had the same look as all of the big financial institutions. I clicked around, added a handful of coins to a shopping cart, and clicked purchase, expecting to find a checkout on the next screen where I could do the math and input payment details.

Instead, the site showed me a congratulatory message, and an email soon arrived with strange looking numbers in it. It was explained to me that these were the routing numbers where I needed to wire a large five-figure sum. To my eye, it seemed shady. No thank you, I said. Customer service was either a stern woman with an eastern European accent or a guy with a Jersey accent. Their position was that I had already committed to buy the gold, and they’d send debt collectors after me if I didn’t pay up. But they could cancel the order for only a few thousand dollars. More than a month later, I’m still disputing it and have involved the attorney general’s office in three states.

Men—and it is indeed mostly men—have been wrongly predicting the end of the world for centuries, from Nostradamus and the Millerites through to the panic over Y2K. What is it that makes us want to prepare? Somewhere in the deepest parts of my monkey brain, prepping hits in the same nerve as when we’d build forts as kids and want to see if they’d withstand a good storm. When a man builds a dam, he wants it to hold a flood. So whether the thing you’re prepping for is a big hurricane, a novel coronavirus, or rogue artificial intelligence, the threat is both a source of dread and wonder. For someone who otherwise suffers from depression, it’s extremely stimulating and a little delusional.

After all, it’s a very narrow window of apocalypse that a prepper of my means can fantasize about. If the disruption is too small, I’ll be like the foolish Y2K dad with the basement full of Chef Boyardee. If the disruption is, indeed, the big one, then everyone, including the personal-plane-New Zealand-bunker-rocket-to-the-Moon money, is probably SOL. The rest of us will be left deciding whether to become the crazy gun lady or the person stealing packages off her porch to survive. In which case, why worry about rice and ammunition? I’d be better off living like some of the humans in The Dark Forest, the sequel to The Three-Body Problem. When the aliens finally arrived, they focused on throwing wild parties and having spontaneous orgies.

If the AI apocalypse hits my fantasy sweet spot—a few months of camping at home before humanity surveys our near-misses and reassembles with renewed clarity and purpose—I’ll be prepared. Maybe the worst comes to pass: economic collapse accompanied by novel bio weapons, loose nukes, and total loss of human agency. In that case, I’ll have the petty satisfaction of having been right. I can hit my group chat with the ultimate mic drop. Told ya.

#6566. 31 Thanksgiving Dinner Alternatives to Turkey

Honestly, anything can make for an alternative Thanksgiving dinner. It’s your house, your rules. Our only suggestion: Make it festive, fun, and at least a little decadent.

A classic Thanksgiving menu is all well and good, but one of our colleagues swears by serving nachos on the fourth Thursday of every November. If a big bloomin’ bird just isn’t ca-caw-caw-calling your name this year, serve a whole roast fish, pork tenderloin with sour-sweet cherry sauce, or a flaky carrot Wellington instead.

Or go completely rogue with lobster pasta or a big pot of chili. You can do that. Below, find vegetarian centerpieces, celebratory roasts, chicken dinners, and seafood mains for a Thanksgiving that looks a little different. BA’s Best Pumpkin Pie can stay.

Can carrots really count as a main course? They can when they’re roasted, glazed, and tucked into puff pastry with goat cheese, Gruyère, and walnuts. This Wellington feeds 8 to 10.

Red wine, browned mushrooms, pearl onions, and carrots give this meatless braise plenty of heft. Ladle it over mashed potatoes for a vegetarian anchor to your Thanksgiving menu.

Ruffled savoy cabbage, melty cheese, and a buttery cream cheese crust make this free-form tart worthy of the holiday table. Cut generous wedges for dinner and stick with savoy: Ordinary green cabbage won’t work here.

A make-ahead casserole, like this pumpkin-infused strata scented with nutmeg and herbs and balanced by sharp cheddar, is just what your holiday schedule needs. Assemble it the night before; bake it on Thanksgiving.

Turkey isn’t the only holiday cooking project worth clearing the counter for. Delicate homemade crepes are rolled around ricotta, mozzarella, and Parmesan, then baked in marinara. Make the batter and filling a day ahead to split up the work.

Kale, pinto beans, and charred poblanos make these cheesy enchiladas a satisfying holiday main for four to six. Get a head start by making the charred salsa verde up to three days ahead.

This autumnal risotto works as a standalone dinner or alongside your favorite Thanksgiving sides. Set the table with shallow bowls and pick a fall salad full of color and crunch to balance the buttery rice.

British beef Wellington meets Cantonese barbecue-style pork in Peter Som’s pastry-wrapped centerpiece. A shiitake mushroom filling and gravy made from the marinade complete the picture; assemble the Wellington a day ahead.

These impossibly tender short ribs are begging to be served with mashed potatoes and buttery milk buns with garlic butter. Give them what they want—and give yourself a head start by braising the ribs the day before Thanksgiving.

Brisket more your speed? Try our Brisket Bourguignon →

Turkey skin has competition. Tender pork belly, crisp crackling, and a hard cider pan sauce make a persuasive case for skipping the bird. Pass the chile vinegar to cut through the richness; this roast feeds 8 to 12.

Ayesha Curry’s spice-crusted prime rib takes its cues from her mother’s braised oxtails, with habanero crema on the side. Prefer a simpler garlic-and-rosemary approach? Try this Low-and-Slow Rib Roast.

For a roast-and-sides Thanksgiving without the turkey, garlic-and-rosemary-rubbed beef tenderloin makes an excellent centerpiece. Rosemary butter dresses the sliced roast, while tangy horseradish yogurt gives everyone something to swipe their next bite through.

Toasted rice, fried onions, and garlic form a dark, peppery crust on this slow-braised pork shoulder. Set out the big platter and pass the coconut-vinegar pan sauce; this roast feeds 8 to 12.

Maybe save the brown sugar-glazed ham for Christmas? This whole leg of lamb makes for a centerpiece that’s just as showstopping. And, like ham and turkey, leftover lamb can be deliciously repurposed in sandwiches.

A platter of sliced pork tenderloin with glossy cherries and browned shallots has plenty of holiday presence without a long roast. Honey and red wine vinegar give the sauce its sweet-sour bite, and frozen cherries are welcome here.

If you’re going to make tamales, it’s a good idea to make a lot of them. Better yet, turn the process into a party, with everyone spreading masa and folding corn husks around the red chile pork filling.

This pasta packs a whole spectrum of holiday flavors into each bite, with crumbles of Italian sausage, shreds of brussels sprouts, and toasted pecans. Streamlining dinner into one dish leaves you more time for Thanksgiving pies.

For some people, spending all Thanksgiving in the kitchen sounds like a good time. For everyone else, there’s this beef-and-bean chili. A can of pumpkin purée thickens the broth, keeping things seasonal without calling for a single roasting pan.

Give homemade fried chicken an even more festive angle with sage and thyme in the dredge and cranberry-mustard sauce for dipping. Start the buttermilk marinade the day before.

This whole roast duck comes with a built-in Thanksgiving side: The duck fat drippings go into basmati rice that cooks while the bird rests. Plan for an overnight dry brine before the glossy pomegranate-honey glaze gets its moment.

Cooking for a smaller crowd? This skillet delivers the stuffing and the bird—chicken thighs, in this case—in one tidy package. Rendered chicken fat enriches the boxed stuffing mix, with dried cranberries and lemon zest brightening things up.

Two diminutive birds make a festive roast for four. A fiery guajillo chile, ginger, and vinegar marinade flavors both the hens and the potatoes beneath them, so the platter arrives with its own very good side.

You just need to make green beans, because this Thanksgiving main is already a two-in-one: Thinly sliced potatoes cook beneath a whole chicken, catching its drippings and crisping around the edges in the same cast-iron skillet.

If your Thanksgiving table could use a little red sauce (and spice), skip the whole bird in favor of this take on chicken parm. Gochujang and gochugaru bring the heat; melted mozzarella keeps things gloriously gooey.

José Andrés turns chicken wings and a colorful assortment of vegetables into a grand centerpiece, with saffron and smoked paprika flavoring the rice. You’ll need a 15" paella pan or comparably sized two-handled cast-iron or cast-aluminum pan.

There’s nothing like pasta to stretch a spendy ingredient (hello, lobster). Serve with a big crunchy salad with Italian dressing and garlic confit toast that diners can pass around for Thanksgiving party vibes.

Presenting a whole fish at the holiday table is wildly celebratory, even when you’re cooking for just two or three. Bring out lettuce wraps, kimchi, rice, and ssamjang so everyone can build each bite a little differently.

A large roasted salmon fillet looks right at home on a holiday platter, especially under a crunchy, garlicky nut salsa. Make the salsa up to four days ahead, then roast the fish when it’s time for dinner.

The stuffing doesn’t have to be a side. Here, crushed boxed stuffing mix joins Parmesan, lemon zest, and parsley in a crisp crust for mustard-coated white fish. Dinner lands on the table in 25 minutes.

This dark, glossy coconut caramel—savory with fish sauce and garlic, sharp with pickled jalapeño brine—turns pan-seared salmon into a holiday-worthy main. Serve with rice to catch every last bit of sauce.

Like many of the best Thanksgiving dishes, this one starts with a good stock. Carla Hall builds a fennel potlikker with celery, onions, and Pernod before layering those flavors into a hearty bowl of shrimp and grits.

#6564. How to Improve Brain Health with 5 Daily Exercises

Brain health isn’t just an issue for the elderly. Maybe you've experienced the first subtle signs of decline. Sometimes it’s a name that’s on the tip of your tongue. Or perhaps you've read a news story in the morning that you can't remember by the evening. It could be that you're feeling increasingly mentally fatigued after a typical day spent dealing with emails, text messages, phone calls, and constant interruptions.

The good news is that you can take steps to keep your mind sharp. “Our brain needs to be stimulated, at any age," says Giuseppe Alfredo Iannoccari, a neuropsychologist, professor at the University of Milan, and president of Assomensana, an association founded in Monza, Italy in 2004 to promote cognitive health. Routines help conserve mental energy, while new experiences force it to work,” says Giuseppe Alfredo Iannoccari, a neuropsychologist, professor at the University of Milan. While working with people suffering from neurodegenerative diseases, including Alzheimer’s, he came up with the idea to create a gym for the brain. “I asked myself what could be done earlier, when people are still healthy,” he said. His studies led him to develop a protocol that anyone can integrate into their daily routine.

The method is based on the principle of neuroplasticity—that is, the brain’s ability to modify its connections in response to learning and experience. This ability persists throughout one’s entire life, although it changes with age. Today, Iannocari's courses consist of weekly 90-minute sessions in groups of up to fifteen participants. Each session features about ten exercises focused on memory, attention, language, reasoning, creativity, and other cognitive skills. At the beginning and end of the program, twelve mental functions are assessed to measure their progress. “In our tests, we observe an average improvement in the overall cognitive efficiency index of 25–30%," says Iannoccari. "Some functions, such as attention and language, respond particularly well. Others, such as logical reasoning and prose memory, require more intensive work.” These results are based on the association’s experience and should not be interpreted as a percentage reduction in the risk of dementia. The World Health Organization’s guidelines, updated in 2026, acknowledge the potential benefits of cognitive training, while emphasizing that evidence regarding the long-term prevention of cognitive decline remains limited.

When it comes to our ability to concentrate, Iannoccari points to one culprit at the center of our modern lives. “Sometimes we feel tired not because we’ve done too many things, but because we’ve switched what we were doing too many times," he says. “Constantly switching from one task to another is more tiring than focusing on the same activity for an extended period.” A stream of notifications, information to process, and the need to respond quickly to various requests put our attention to the test above all else. “It’s the foundation of all cognitive processes. When it’s fragmented, even the quality of the information we’re able to acquire deteriorates.”

And then there’s AI, which promises to free us from an ever-increasing number of tasks. What are the consequences for our brains? “If we ask artificial intelligence to compare two tables, perform an analysis, and write a report, we get the work done in a few minutes that would previously have taken an entire day," says Iannoccari. “Saving work also means reducing some mental activity. But it depends on how we use these tools.”

For Iannoccari, the key is to preserve two abilities: critical thinking and analysis. “We must know how to formulate questions, and this requires familiarity with the subject,” he says. “Then we must evaluate the answers, recognize any inconsistencies, and verify the information. Only a well-trained mind can spot errors.” This issue also applies to seemingly beneficial habits, such as reading books or solving crossword puzzles.“ Reading is invaluable, especially for the emotions it evokes and the worlds it allows us to discover," he says. “But reading doesn’t automatically mean memorizing. If we want to remember what we’ve read, we must do so with the intention of being able to recount it to someone else.” As for puzzle-solving pastimes, “Sudoku trains certain concentration and planning skills, while crossword puzzles stimulate the retrieval of information from memory,” he says. “These are useful activities, but a structured program allows you to work on different skills and gradually increase the difficulty of the exercises.”

In addition to guided sessions, Iannoccari suggests short daily sessions he calls “Brain Breaks”— five-minute breaks for small exercises that counteract brain aging. “If we wait to find five free minutes, we’ll probably never find them.” “We need to make it a habit, just like having a cup of coffee.” Here are five exercises you can try:

Choose a topic—preferably a positive one—read it carefully, and try to recount it to three different people without constantly referring back to the text. “The first time we repeat a piece of information, we’re often uncertain,” says Iannoccari. “The second time, we become clearer and more fluent. The third time, we have another chance to reinforce it in our memory.” It’s an exercise that stimulates what’s known as “prose memory”—the ability to recall and process information we’ve read or heard. “Let’s imagine learning one piece of news a day for 365 days: how much knowledge will we have accumulated?”

For five minutes, write down as many words as possible that start with the letter A, trying to be quick. Repeat the exercise the next day, avoiding words you’ve already used. On the third day, move on to B, and so on. “It’s a way to train verbal fluency and lexical retrieval, particularly useful when we start to experience that ‘word on the tip of my tongue’ phenomenon,” says Iannoccari. The goal is to gradually make the search more challenging by striving to find words that aren’t immediately obvious.

Right-handed people can try performing some simple tasks with their left hand, and vice versa. Open a drawer, move small objects, draw, and gradually try writing. “This new challenge forces the brain to break out of its automatic routines and engage resources we normally use less," he says. “Surprising results can be achieved: people who initially can’t even draw a line gradually learn to write with their other hand.” Of course, it’s best to choose safe activities and proceed without rushing.

How many phone numbers do we still remember? And how often do we rely on the GPS even to get to relatively familiar places? “Before calling someone, I try to remember their number," says Iannoccari. “Before using a calculator, I do the math in my head. Before turning on the GPS, I try to figure out the route.” The same goes for the grocery list. “I write it down so I can be sure I won’t forget anything, but at the supermarket I first try to recall the items. Only then do I check the list.” These are small opportunities to keep practicing skills that we increasingly tend to delegate to digital tools.

Once in bed, instead of focusing on the next day’s commitments, try to mentally retrace the day that just passed. What time did you wake up? What did you eat? Who did you meet? What did you talk about? What details stood out to us? “You have to try to be very detailed,” says Iannoccari. “Often, people who have trouble falling asleep find that this exercise also helps them drift off.”

But there’s another aspect that’s particularly close to his heart. “I find there’s something romantic about it. We live one day after another and often retain almost nothing of them. Reflecting on it means recognizing its value. Every day leaves something behind, like a geological layer deposited on top of the one before it.” This little ritual offers an opportunity to recall the experiences we wish to preserve.

When is the right time to start? “As children,” says Iannoccari. “We encourage them to play sports, but we rarely think about the importance of training mental abilities just as intentionally.” In adult life, of course, exercise, sleep, nutrition, stress management, and social relationships also matter. “But if I had to name three drivers of the mind, I’d choose curiosity, creativity, and emotions."he says. "Curiosity opens us up to new knowledge, creativity allows us to connect that knowledge in original ways, and emotions make experiences more memorable.”

He also notes that, though older age is associated with worse brain function, it's also how we collect the wisdom of lived experiences. “We think an efficient brain is the one we had at twenty, and we lose sight of what we’ve gained by the time we’re sixty or seventy," he says. "When we were young, we may have been faster, but over time we’ve accumulated skills, knowledge, and experience. We possess a much richer worldview.”

The real challenge is to remain present to ourselves and others, valuing who we’ve become.” And perhaps, as the years go by, one of the most important skills is precisely learning to choose where to invest our mental energy. “We meet people who, now that they’re retired, are busier than when they were working. We’ve come to associate efficiency with the number of things we can do, but in doing so, we lose the opportunity to delve deeper, reflect, and let experiences settle. I always say that I don’t pursue nice ideas—I pursue great ideas. Because there are so many nice ideas, and they risk scattering our energy in a thousand different directions.” “With age,” concludes Iannoccari, “we have a great privilege: the ability to choose.”

A version of this story originally appeared in GQ Italia.

#6563. 2026 Was the Year of the Fashion Bride

If—for a certain set of cool, young designers—doing bridal was once thought uncool, 2026 may have been the year that finally put that notion to rest.

We’ve been seeing the shift for years now: For many brides, the wedding-day dream has gone beyond the beautiful, white, traditionally “bridal” wedding dress. Increasingly, brides want something, well, cool—an expression of their personal brand and sensibility, whether that means a painstakingly sourced archival look or a custom piece by an unexpected designer. This year, that trend was on full display, as wedding fashion increasingly became a stage and cultural touchpoint for brides and designers alike.

2026 was a banner year for high-profile weddings and celebrity brides wearing everything from romantic gowns to razor-sharp suits: Zendaya and Tom Holland, Dua Lipa and Callum Turner, Dove Cameron and Damiano David, Cristiano Ronaldo and Georgina Rodríguez, Emma Roberts and Cody John, Karl-Anthony Towns and Jordyn Woods, to name just a few.

And that’s without even mentioning the “royal wedding” of Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce. While the photos are yet to be released (and if you ask Swift bestie Dakota Johnson, they never will be), we do know that Swift became Jonathan Anderson’s first celebrity bride, a move that had people feverishly searching for clues at his Dior Haute Couture show in July. Could it be that white chiffon and degradé lace final gown, which later graced the runway at Vogue World: Milan? Nothing was revealed, apart from Anderson telling Women’s Wear Daily, “It was a joy to work with her. We became very good friends,” and “It’s an emotional thing doing someone’s wedding.”

Dua Lipa’s August wedding, meanwhile, was a fashion extravaganza, starting with a custom Schiaparelli white skirt suit, designed by creative director Daniel Roseberry. Who can forget the image of the pop star, beaming under a burst of confetti as she walked out of the town hall as a newlywed? Her suit was inspired by Bianca Jagger’s bridal look for her wedding to Mick Jagger in Saint-Tropez on May 12, 1971, perhaps the ultimate cool-girl bridal nod. Lipa rounded out her bridal looks with a white leather Bottega Veneta custom gown by Louise Trotter, and a Chanel haute couture gown for her main wedding dress.

Beyond the celeb wedding world, this year saw rising stars and in-demand designers put forward bridal looks, some for the first time. Dilara Findikoglu launched her first bridal capsule, a rule-breaking, lingerie-forward offering adapted from her ready-to-wear line, with campaign photos of models smashing plates, smoking, and mounting their grooms. (“I really believe that the power of my clothes is to bring out the uniqueness in someone,” Findikoglu previously told Vogue. “That’s exactly why they became Dilara Brides: to reveal the most unique version of who they already are.”)

Dilara Findikoglu’s debut bridal collection.

Batsheva debuted her first bridal collection at New York’s Bridal Fashion Week. Christopher John Rogers solidified his status as a sought-after designer for stylish brides, including Vogue fashion market director Naomi Elizée Blue, TikTok brand strategist Ali Lebow, and film director Pam Nasr. In an interview with The New York Times about his rising profile in the wedding world, Rogers even teased his very own bridal collection.

Naomi Elizée Blue in Christopher John Rogers.

CFDA/Vogue Fashion Funders Zoe Gustavia Anna Whalen and Miss Claire Sullivan created custom bridal looks for Architectural Digest senior design editor Hannah Martin and the artist Tourmaline, respectively. Martin’s gown was inspired by a look from Whalen’s spring 2025 collection, featuring a corseted bodice with a padded hip. Whalen previously told Vogue about why she decided to take on a bridal client, a rare move for her. “It aligns so much with my general ethos of garments being these weighted, emotional objects,” Whalen said. “So when it’s the right fit, being able to create that with such intention for somebody else is so beautiful.”

Tourmaline (right) in Miss Claire Sullivan.

Elsewhere, Raul Lopez dressed his friends Juice Rodriguez and Cristal Veras in coordinated Luar for their New York wedding. Gabbriette became the first bride for Matières Fécales, the cult Paris label whose show Rihanna attended in September. And Colleen Allen, winner of the 2026 CFDA Emerging Designer of the Year Award, has quietly become the fashion girls’ dream wedding dress designer, after making a custom look for Charli xcx’s wedding reception last year.

“Bridal” no longer means just one thing. For independent designers, it can be a playground to express something new, a platform for their brand, and, as Joe Bobowicz observed in a Vogue Business article, a dependable revenue stream. And as people expand their ideas of what a wedding can look like—donning colorful gowns in every color from butter yellow to pink to black, and playing with material and silhouette—as we head into 2027, the future of bridal style has never been more thrillingly uncertain.
