#6549. How We Brought a Taste of Maine to Bon Appétit LIVE

Attendees of Bon Appétit Live experienced a taste of Maine through a hands-on lobster cooking class and a demonstration of wild blueberry cornmeal shortcakes, both hosted by Visit Maine.

The class, Lobster 101, was led by Bon Appétit manager of audience strategy Carly Westerfield and Krista Tripp, founder of Aphrodite Oysters in South Thomaston, Maine. Attendees learned how to break down a whole, steamed two-pound Maine lobster and transform the meat into a rich, creamy lobster dip—ideal for holiday hosting. Guests then enjoyed the fruits of their labor, sampling the freshly made dip with Ritz crackers before tasting oysters.

Tripp explained that her oysters, cultivated in the cold tidal waters of the Lower Weskeag River, take three years to reach maturity. Known for their distinctive fluted shells, they offer a briny, mineral-rich flavor balanced by a mellow sweetness.

After years as a lobster harvester, Tripp started Aphrodite Oysters to diversify her lobster business and has since shifted her focus to oyster cultivation full-time. She’s come to appreciate the many environmental benefits of farming and consuming them. Her oysters filter up to 50 gallons of water a day, taking in nitrogen and sequestering some for their growing shells. “Eating an oyster is contributing to the environment,” she declared. Indeed, water test scores have improved at her farm, demonstrating that bivalves help create a healthier ecosystem.

Before the end of the class, a few brave attendees volunteered to shuck their first oysters. Krista guided them through the process, demonstrating how to safely do it at home by protecting the hand holding the shellfish with a towel and gently working the knife into the hinge until the shell released. The well-earned reward was another taste of the Penobscot Bay, as fresh and pristine as the waters themselves.

Later in the day, guests in the Demo Kitchen were treated to Cornmeal Shortcakes with Blueberry Compote, prepared by Bon Appétit senior Test Kitchen editor Jesse Szewczyk. The compote featured wild Maine blueberries from Brodis Blueberries, a multigenerational family farm in Hope, Maine, stewarded by Ron Howard and his family. Howard joined Szewczyk for the demo, where he shared that 99% of the wild blueberries grown and harvested in the United States come from Maine. Attendees learned that they have been growing since the end of the Ice Age, when the tenacious plants, fortified by ericoid mycorrhizal fungi, began to grow and colonize the newly exposed land as glaciers retreated. An important food source for Native Americans, wild blueberries were valued by Indigenous communities for their nutritional benefits well before the modern superfood movement.

Speaking passionately, Howard discussed the many challenges facing Maine growers, including tariffs and currency exchange fluctuations, particularly the impact of a stronger Canadian dollar. Like many Maine farmers, the family has had to get creative. Howard invested in new equipment, including a more efficient type of harvester that allowed the business to scale up and sell to retailers. They created a shelf-stable, freeze-dried product with no added ingredients, allowing them to ship their product beyond the local area. Howard and his son started a distillery, where they use wild blueberries to make an eau de vie and vodka. They have also begun hosting a Wild Blueberry Weekend, opening the doors to the farm and educating the public about the unique benefits of their crop and their growing process.

Carolann Ouellette, director of the Maine Office of Tourism, emphasized that visiting Maine and engaging with local growers and producers such as Howard and Tripp was the best way to experience the state’s diverse bounty. “The relationship between people and nature is inseparable, and stewardship is an important part of the state's identity,” she reflected. Ouellette grew up in New Jersey but relocated to Maine over 40 years ago. Her family used to visit Maine when she was a child, and she recalls those experiences vividly: “As a kid, I remember, when you get to Maine, you can smell the pie or smell the spruce.” It’s those potent memories that drew her to the state permanently, a place she described as “filled with hardworking, welcoming communities that depend on one another.”

A few years ago, Visit Maine began placing greater emphasis on the state’s culinary identity. Ouellette said that awareness of Maine as a food destination continues to grow, “Sea to table with local ingredients is what we were doing before it was a thing.” Beyond the lobster, Visit Maine has been intentional about showcasing the breadth of the state’s agricultural, fishing, and heritage industries. Apples, potatoes, kelp, seaweed, and grains are just a few of the local ingredients featured in Visit Maine’s newsletter and Bountiful Plate video series, which highlights food and beverage producers throughout the state. Ouellette noted that Maine’s food culture is more diverse than many people expect, and its abundance of local products has attracted an interesting mix of exceptional chefs, many of whom are deeply embedded in their communities. Ouellette cited Tripp’s practice of personally delivering her oysters to local restaurants as an example of how the hospitality ecosystem is interconnected.

Most important, Ouellette emphasized that sustainability and stewardship are central to the state’s approach to its food systems and relationship with the landscape. “You can’t get much fresher than food in Maine,” she concluded.

Bon Appétit LIVE 2026 was sponsored by East Fork, Visit Maine, and S.Pellegrino® Sparkling Natural Mineral Water with thanks to All-Clad, As Ever, Bachan’s, Better Sour, Field Company, Floura, Gimme Seaweed, GOODLES, Graza, Hedley & Bennett, Kann Coffee, Material Kitchen, Misen, Owala®, Rip Van, SharkNinja, and Staub.

#6545. Soothing Rice Porridge

This is a Japanese-style rice porridge known as okayu. I ate this every morning in the early weeks of postpartum after my first daughter was born. It’s what our family reaches for whenever we need a simple, nourishing dish that warms from the inside out. For the smoothest porridge, let the rice soak in cold water before cooking.

If you have time, soak the rice, which makes the texture softer and can aid in digestion. Place washed rice in a bowl and pour in water to cover by 1". Soak at least 30 minutes and up to 4 hours. Drain off excess water before starting the recipe. The wakame seaweed, which you’ve probably had in miso soup, can typically be found dried anywhere Asian groceries are available.

In The Fourth Trimester, we ask parents: What meal nourished you after welcoming your baby? This month it’s a cozy rice porridge by Eating at Home cookbook author Trinity Mouzon Wofford. Read more: Breakfast at Home, After Birth at Home.

Combine 1 cup short-grain rice, washed, soaked if desired, ¼ cup dried wakame (seaweed), 1 Tbsp. dried red shiso, and 6 cups low-sodium broth (any kind) or water in a large donabe, medium Dutch oven, or other heavy pot. Cover and bring to a boil over medium-high heat (you’ll hear bubbling). Uncover and stir, making sure nothing is stuck to bottom of pot. Cover and reduce heat to low. Continue to cook porridge 30 minutes more (resist the urge to peek).

Remove pot from heat and let porridge sit (still covered) 10 minutes. Uncover and stir. Rice grains should be cooked through, broken open, and creamy, but porridge should still be fairly loose. Season porridge with fine sea salt.

Ladle porridge into bowls and serve, topped with toasted sesame seeds, toasted sesame oil, and/or thinly sliced scallions.

#6544. 36 Best Sweaters for Men 2025, According to GQ Editors

The best sweaters for men are, next to a hearty soup, the coziest, most comforting things of the colder seasons. And like a delicious bowl of life-giving soup, sweaters come in a myriad of styles, each with their own distinct combination of flavors, textures, and cultural significance. A classic merino wool crewneck sweater is the chicken noodle soup of the knitwear realm while a potato leek soup is more like a mohair turtleneck with its velvety, creamy texture. A hot bowl of thick, savory congee parallels the heavy-gauge knit and cold-busting insulation of a Cowichan cardigan. But whether it’s a quarter zip or menudo, cashmere or kimchi jjigae, navigating the endless amount of options can be tough, especially on an empty stomach.

Consider what you’re trying to achieve with a sweater. That can be both literal and metaphorical Are you trying to channel the GOAT decade, dripping in ’90s nostalgia? Or are you gearing up for holiday fits and festive chaos? Or maybe you just need a workhorse sweater that looks great with most outfits and will keep you warm three seasons out of the year. Whatever the case may be, you’ve come to the right place and while we can’t tell you what your palate will like, we can walk you through the menu.

Like Michael Jordan dropping his famous “I'm back” statement, the V-neck is ready to reclaim its menswear throne as the MVP of your sweater rotation. You might be tempted to start with the obvious play, like layering one over a crisp button-up shirt, maybe letting the shirt's collar laze insouciantly over the V. But follow the leads of the romcom stars and airport travel gods from the '90s: there’s something casually chic about a plain white T-shirt peeking out at clavicle height.

It's the Champion sweatshirt you wish you could live in, but refined enough to handle weekday meetings and weekend coffee dates. Crewneck sweaters can come in more flavors than Baskin-Robbins, and can be made from jacquard knits (see below), thick cable knits (also below), or damn near any other woven fabric. Our only suggestion: while there’s nothing wrong with a gets-the-job-done heather gray colorway, don't shortchange yourself by avoiding more adventurous colors.

The sweater vest moment has been ramping up for several seasons and while we may be at peak vest, we're still totally here for it. It’s a notoriously tricky knit to style, but one that can actually add a ton of versatility to your closet. Whatever's underneath—a striped button-up shirt, a tee, nothing but your guns—gets a supporting actor nod. For extra warmth, the sweater vest fits well under both cropped outerwear and tailoring, like a suit jacket or sport coat, without adding unnecessary bulk. And it can turn a simple white tee-and-jeans combo (maybe add some loafers?) into an unstoppable farmers-market-to-cocktail-hour fit.

Depending on the weather and your location's relation to the equator, a lightweight cardi will be the only “coat” you need. If temperatures are still moderately warm, opt for a cardigan made from breathable linen or cotton, paired with a button-up shirt and relaxed-fit chinos for a laid-back, preppy look. Once temps start to cool down, upgrade your winter wardrobe with a heavyweight wool sweater—maybe with a scarf-replacing shawl collar—to stay nice and toasty.

Whether you prefer a quarter-zip, half-zip, or full-zip, the knitwear of choice for dads all over is back. Look past its dorky nature and a zip sweater can be clean as a whistle and more stylish than you remember. Think of it as a convertible, but for your torso. Show off a little T-shirt and a necklace underneath, or zip that thing all the way to the top for a riff on the turtleneck that trades stuffy for sporty.

It's a sweater with a collar, ya know what I mean? But in all seriousness, the polo sweater is even more solutions-oriented than its short-sleeve sibling. It instantly adds a touch of dressiness to an outfit without having to go full button down and tie, all while maintaining Olympic levels of cozy. Pair it with some non-jean pants for the easiest, comfiest Monday-through-Friday outfit in your arsenal. Or, let it anchor your out-of-office—the brighter and bolder, the better.

Blending form (straight lines to elongate that torso) with functionality (gotta keep ya neck warm) with sexiness (just look at it), the turtleneck remains a humble wardrobe heavyweight. A simple rib knit version can do damn near anything, anytime, but don't sleep on a turtleneck with a crochet, cable, or jacquard knit. Just ask The Rock, Michael B. Jordan, Tom Holland, or any of Hollywood's many leading men who figured out long ago that a turtleneck turns up the heat in more ways than the obvious.

The quintessentially preppy cable knit is the sweater most likely to say it “went to school in Cambridge.” You can lean into the Ivy League energy, or mix-and-match other styles. Similar, yet completely distinct, is the fisherman sweater or the Aran sweater. Originating from the western cost of Ireland, Aran sweaters have their roots in fishing and use intricate cable knit designs. A key difference aside from their origins is that fisherman sweaters are always hearty, chunky knits with thicker cable-knit designs.

Like the Aran sweater, the Fair Isle sweater is also named for an island (in the Shetlands, off the coast of Scotland). This time, the signature designs are less about texture, and more about the color, with traditional patterns knit into the wool. While it’s been unfairly dragged into the whole “Christmas sweater" conversation, Fair Isles deserve to be worn for as many months as you need the toastiness.

As mentioned, you should go into this like you’re adopting a dog, not like a kid in a candy store. It can be satisfying for a moment to pick up the first pretty thing you see, but a crash follows the rush and before you know it, you’ve got a pile of sweaters that are either too warm, too itchy, or just don’t fit right. Don’t make that mistake, here’s what to look out for.

Cotton: We’re not going to belabor the benefits of cotton—the natural fiber is breathable, affordable, washes easily (though careful with the dryer—always read that tag), and gentle on sensitive skin. You can’t go wrong with a cotton sweater any time of the year, but if you’re looking for a transitional layer that’ll keep you warm now and comfortably cool later, it's hard to top cotton.

Wool: Not to mix our species, but wool can be a chameleon. The sheep-borne spectrum runs from airy and light to thick and hefty. But all of it is uniquely adept at regulating temperatures, so you'll stay warm without burning up. While you have to be a little more delicate on the upkeep (almost definitely no dryer), your tough-as-nails wool knit can last you for decades—literally—with some conscientious upkeep.

Cashmere: It used to be that the average “nice” wool sweater was made of merino wool or lambswool, and cashmere was reserved for the rich guys. A few decades of commodifying the luxury fiber has helped bring it to more affordable tiers. Though careful what you pay for: cheap cashmere pills easily, can feel oily, and won't last nearly as long as the good stuff.

Mohair: Shaggier and a hair (sorry) lighter than wool, a mohair sweater isn't afraid to make a statement. Chances are you’ve seen NBA elites sporting the ubiquitous horizontal-striped Marni cardigan, or you've spotted a number of Needle’s eyeball-popping patterned versions out in the wild. Though it's worth pointing out, you can absolutely find more relaxed versions—in both cardigan and button-free variations—if you're not trying to flex for ESPN's cameras.

Synthetics: More often than not, you’ll encounter sweaters that blend man-made materials like polyester, acrylic, and elastane. These materials can help give a sweater desirable qualities like softness, moisture-wicking, insulation, and stretch. They’re also cheaper to produce. While that doesn’t always translate into a low-quality product, it does mean that a brand is cutting costs which often result in an inferior garment.

Beyond the material that’s used to make a sweater, the yarns and gauge of those yarns influence light or heavy the final product will be. The fibers are spun into yarns, which are then knit together to form a sweater. The gauge refers to the thickness of those yarns and can be the difference between an airy spring sweater and a chunky deep-winter cardigan. The thicker the gauge, the heavier and warmer the sweater will be.

The balance between material and fabric weight is a delicate one. So when you’re deciding on a sweater, remember that a heavy cotton sweater can potentially be just as warm as a thin merino wool sweater or that a densely knit cashmere sweater will be warmer than an equally chunky cotton alternative.

Aside from the rarer summer knitwear, sweaters are made for cold weather. So fit is especially important considering you’ll be layering your sweater over and under other garments. Consider whether you’ll be wearing it over a button-up and tie or just a simple T-shirt. For the slightly reckless, slightly sexier among us, also consider whether you’ll be wearing it without any undershirt at all.

Same goes for the outer layers that’ll go on top. A chunky sweater is satisfying and cozy as hell, but can easily become unwieldy if you’re trying to stuff it under a tailored blazer. When it comes to fit, there’s no single best silhouette, but there are a couple of rules of thumb if you can’t make heads or tails of it. Make sure the shoulder seams hit just past your shoulder bones, that the sleeves reach to your wrist bones, and that the hem sits right around your hips.

#6543. Maple-Sausage Breakfast Casserole

Inspired by the iconic egg and sausage sandwich on a pancake bun, this breakfast casserole is cheesy and just a smidge sweet from the brushing of maple butter at the very end. Destined for holiday brunch tables everywhere and best enjoyed while you’re still in pajamas, this cozy bake will feed a full house. (Don’t be surprised if you find yourself making it again long after the last guest leaves though!)

More high-protein breakfast recipes here.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 400°. Lightly coat a 13x9" baking dish with nonstick vegetable oil spray. Whisk 2½ cups (313 g) all-purpose flour, ¼ cup (50 g) sugar, 2 Tbsp. baking powder, 2 tsp. freshly ground pepper, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a large bowl to combine. Set aside.

Cook 2 lb. breakfast sausage, casings removed if needed, in a large skillet set over medium-high heat, stirring and breaking into small pieces with a wooden spoon, until browned and cooked through, 10–12 minutes. Using a slotted spoon, transfer sausage to a small plate, leaving fat behind. Pour fat into a heatproof measuring glass. You want ½ cup fat; spoon out any excess or pour in vegetable oil as needed if you don’t have enough. Stir 2 large eggs and 2 cups whole milk into fat. Let sausage cool slightly, then crumble into small, even pieces with your hands.

Pour fat mixture into reserved dry ingredients and stir until just combined and no large dry pockets of flour remain (batter may be thin and lumpy; it’ll be fine). Set aside ½ cup sausage and ½ cup cheese from 8 oz. sharp yellow cheddar, coarsely grated (about 2 cups), for topping, then add remaining sausage and cheddar to batter and stirring until evenly distributed.

Scrape batter into prepared baking dish and evenly scatter reserved sausage and cheese over. Bake casserole until top springs back when gently pressed with your finger and a tester inserted into the center comes out with just a few moist crumbs attached, 20–30 minutes.

Just before casserole is done, heat 2 Tbsp. pure maple syrup and 2 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a small skillet over medium, stirring occasionally, until butter is melted, about 2 minutes.

Brush maple butter over casserole and let cool 10 minutes. Cut into squares. Serve with more maple syrup and butter alongside.

#6540. Apple Juice Bread

A simple swap from water to apple juice transforms this basic bread recipe into a subtly sweet loaf that is perfect to tear into at breakfast time with a smear of good butter on top, but it also takes a PB&J to the next level. The subtle, but unmistakable, undercurrent of apple sweetness struck me as a bit of a magic trick in a bread that, otherwise, to the eye and hand was just a soft white loaf.

I first encountered the idea at the small four-seat teppanyaki restaurant in the back of the Suiran Hotel in Kyoto, Japan, where chef Tsubasa Yamaguchi served it before my first course; it was a perfect way to start the meal. When I asked him what he did differently to prepare it, he said he just took the same rustic bread recipe he baked elsewhere and used apple juice in place of water. I was incredulous. That was it? The same amount? The same technique? Yes and yes, he said. I was hooked. It turns out the water-to-juice switcheroo gives an added taste of fall without taking anything away from the shape and texture. It’s become an instant favorite at my house both breakfast and lunch, and I expect it will be at yours.

Take care when you’re lowering the bread into the Dutch oven; it is a slightly nerve-wracking moment but a little attention is all that’s needed. You can do it!

More apple recipes here: 37 Apple Desserts That Make Us Want to Pick the Whole Orchard

Mix 4 cups (500 g) all-purpose flour, 1¾ cups apple juice, 1 Tbsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 1 Tbsp. sugar, and one ¼-oz. envelope instant yeast (about 2¼ tsp.) in a large bowl just until flour is hydrated and a very shaggy dough forms, about 1 minute. Cover bowl with plastic wrap and let dough sit at room temperature 15 minutes.

Set a small bowl of room-temperature water on work surface for easy reaching. Uncover dough, dip your hand in water and stretch one side of dough up and over to meet opposite side; turn bowl 90°. Repeat 3 more times, turning bowl 90° after each fold. (This constitutes 1 full fold.) If dough doesn’t always stretch to meet opposite side, just aim for the middle. Wet your hands and shake off excess water any time dough begins to feel sticky. Cover dough and let sit 30 minutes (set a timer). Repeat folding process to make 1 full fold. Re-cover and let dough sit another 30 minutes. Repeat folding process and resting one more time. By the last fold, dough should be significantly smoother and tighter.

Transfer dough to a generously floured surface, dust with flour, and shape into a tight ball. Dust dough with more flour. Dust a kitchen towel with flour and place inside a high-sided bowl to line. Arrange dough, seam side up, in bowl on top of towel. Tightly cover bowl with plastic wrap and let dough sit in a warm spot until puffy, about 45 minutes.

Place a rack in middle of oven, then set a large ovenproof Dutch oven with a lid on it; preheat oven to 400°. Place a 12" square of parchment paper on a flat surface. Cut a 2"-long slit in each corner toward the center. Very carefully, tip dough out onto center of parchment, trying your best not to deflate it or ruin its shape. (It’s easiest to place parchment on a flat plate so you can easily turn dough out of bowl.) Working very quickly and using a pair of kitchen shears lightly coated in vegetable oil, cut an X in center of bread. Remove pot from oven and very carefully lower dough into pot. Cover pot and return to oven.

Bake bread 35 minutes. Uncover pot, reduce oven temperature to 375°, and continue to bake bread until crust is deeply browned, 35–40 minutes more. Carefully tip loaf out onto a wire rack and let cool at least 1 hour before slicing.

Do Ahead: Bread can be baked 3 days ahead. Let cool completely; store airtight at room temperature.

#6539. Doing Crime Barely Covers My Menswear Habit in 'GTA VI'

I am still slightly delirious. When GTA 6 came out at midnight last week, I played it for eight hours straight, all in the name of real, boots-on-the-ground journalism. Well, there was a quick power nap somewhere around 5 a.m., but otherwise I've been working very hard. I have a new wardrobe and some concerns about the price of digital jorts.

Most people will have spent their first-ever session getting through the missions, exploring the map, and finding out what Jason and Lucia have got themselves into. Not me. My main goal was to visit as many shops as possible. It's been 13 years since GTA 5; I wanted to see what had happened to the menswear.

Before we get into it, you should know: Your in-game clothes matter more than ever compared to other entries in the Grand Theft Auto universe. As I wrote last week, the new “heat” system lets cops remember what you were wearing, so losing them doesn't necessarily mean you're in the clear. Changing your hat or sunglasses won't clear the clothing clue, either. You need a full fit change. So technically, all this shopping could help me get away with something. That's my justification, anyway.

Unfortunately, even virtual shopping requires cold, hard cash—and early on, that takes considerably more effort than I'd hoped. You start with almost nothing, spending much of the opening stretch around Key Lento in swampy Mariana County. I'd gone in expecting to buy loads of clothes. Instead, I was checking what I could afford.

My first opportunity came in a random gun shop that also sold some workwear. I had a quick browse then went straight for the camo shorts. Back in August, British GQ's senior style editor Mahalia Chang declared that “camo shorts are fucking back, baby,” having watched Jason spend much of the trailer wearing them. Who was I to argue?

Nearby, in Hamlet, I found a few thrift shops and picked up a battered chore jacket with more than a little Carhartt Detroit about it. It looked properly used, which suited both my budget and the general condition of my pickup. I bought a watch, too, but more on that another time.

I was already getting quite into it. I was comparing pieces, checking prices, and deciding what could wait. There were clothes I wanted and clothes I could afford. Annoyingly, the game understood the difference.

I bought a trucker cap at one point and was very happy with it. Over the summer, I wrote about wanting to give them another go despite having a head my mates call “a sniper's dream.” Jason doesn't have that problem (in a metaphorical sense, anyway), so I thought I'd let him enjoy one. Shortly afterwards, a gang of lads picked a fight with me, punched me, and knocked it off his head. I fled, only realizing once I was safely away that I hadn't picked it back up. I'd barely had a chance to enjoy it. I hope one of them's wearing it at least.

After a few missions, I finally had enough money to justify another shopping trip. I got into my beaten-up pickup and headed downtown, where the prices started getting a little more serious. Denim jackets were around $120. A pair of dark wash jorts I really liked cost $45, which was slightly more than I wanted to spend.

I appreciate that this is a game in which you can steal a car, and I was still having a small financial discussion with myself about the price of shorts. For a game called Grand Theft Auto, I'd done surprisingly little car stealing in the time I'd been playing.

The map is absolutely massive, and there almost 70 clothing stores to work through, so visiting everything was never gonna happen in one sitting. Cars now use fuel, too. Driving miles out of your way to look at a jacket comes with an additional expense, and I had to leave enough money to get home.

There was a reason to keep exploring, though. I went into another shop expecting more of the same and realized the stock was different, so now I wanted to check the other shops before buying anything. Apparently, I'd waited 13 years to recreate how I spend my Saturdays.

Naturally, I decided to drive to Ocean Beach, a more expensive part of the city where I had very little business shopping. Inside Nola, the person at the till looked me up and down in my shitty workwear and asked, “Eh, are you looking for somebody?”

It was an impressively efficient assessment of my finances. Nola felt a little like Casablanca, the French-Moroccan label known for colorful prints, sportswear, and clothes that suggest a considerably nicer holiday than the one you're on. I'd previously called Hawaiian shirts “the unofficial uniform of Vice City.” Here, joining in cost about $330. Blazers were about $430. I could look, provided I didn't get any dirt on anything.

Then I accidentally punched the shop assistant; I'm still getting used to the controls. At least, I think it was an accident. Either way, I had to flee before I could give the blazers much consideration. When I came back later, the store was temporarily closed. I hope it wasn't due to staff injuries.

Other boutiques were even less accommodating to my balance. Italian house Ferruccio Tucci (probably a GTA-ified Emilio Pucci) had $3,000 suits and $1,200 horsebit loafers. I went in to browse and accidentally bought a pair of $350 shades, which was a very expensive way to learn which button does what. The annoying thing is that they looked genuinely sick—exactly the sort of thing I'd wear IRL, which made it much easier to justify keeping them. Well, that was fuel and dinner gone for the day. At least I could look good while walking home.

Later, driving past Waxman Island, I came across Vice City's Eris flagship. Obviously, I had to go in. For anyone who hasn't spent the past few months staring at fictional trainers, Eris is basically GTA's answer to Nike. Nike takes its name from the Greek goddess of victory; Eris is the goddess of strife and discord. The shoes are often just as recognizable as the joke.

The store kinda reminded me a little of Niketown in London—currently closed for refurbishment—with neon lights and big statues and enough footwear to keep me occupied considerably longer than was sensible. There was the Rise Low, an Air Force 1 lookalike that I ended up getting in two colourways; the Strife 360, with its very Air Max 97-ish shape; and the Rook 1 High, which follows the Air Jordan 1 High. I own more than 400 pairs of sneakers IRL—I probably should've known that going in here would be a problem.

And Eris is only one option. There are alternative sneaker labels, beach shops, souvenir shops, and smaller, DIY-looking streetwear brands all dotted around the city. I'd barely begun working through them. Every time I thought I'd seen enough to stop, there was another shop worth going into.

The most expensive-looking thing I acquired didn't come from a boutique at all. Slight spoiler: A naked man offered to give me his “Crowex” watch after pulling a plastic egg out of his own ass. (Yes, you read that right.) You'll know him when you see him. I'm not gonna go into any more detail, partly because I'm tired and partly because I'd like you to experience that transaction yourself.

Eight hours in, I'd hardly scratched the surface. What surprised me most was how long the expensive stuff felt like it would take to earn. Those suits and loafers were sitting there, available to try, while my balance suggested another few missions first. There's a lot of city left to explore, quite a few shops I want to revisit, and a pair of jorts I'm still thinking about.

For now, though, I need some sleep. And Jason needs to earn back that $350.

A version of this story originally appeared in British GQ.

#6538. Chocolate-Covered Strawberry Turkeys

Turkey is the star of Thanksgiving dinner, but it can also be the star of dessert if you stretch your imagination enough. This idea first gained popularity on TikTok, using chocolate-dipped strawberries, marshmallows, pretzel rods, and melted chocolate to create these adorable little treats.

They're so simple to make: To make a leg, you spear two mini marshmallows with half a pretzel rod, then use kitchen shears to trim the edges into a long oval shape. Repeat for a second leg, then cut one mini marshmallow diagonally in half to make the wings. You'll stick these to the strawberry with a dab of melted chocolate (which acts as your glue), then let that sit to adhere. All that's left is a quick bath in melted chocolate.

#6537. Connor Storrie Mixes a “Mezcal Mandy”—and Addresses His Controversial Buzzcut—for Vogue’s Now Serving

“Let me slip into something a little more comfortable,” Connor Storrie says in Vogue’s latest Now Serving episode, trading his Saint Laurent by Anthony Vaccarello ribbed beige V-neck sweater and belted gray trousers—he deadpans it’s his “Sunday walking around the house look”—for a gleaming gold metallic trench coat and aviator sunglasses. (Storrie eventually switches back to cook, though the energy remains decidedly high-fashion.)

First up, the Heated Rivalry actor—and Vogue’s 2026 Best Dressed cover star—prepares his go-to order on a night out: a “Mezcal Mandy.” Skipping the jigger in favor of an eyeball pour of roughly two shots of mezcal over ice, topped with lime and soda water, Storrie takes a sip—despite the shoot taking place at 10 a.m. “This drink says that I don’t want any sugar in my system, but I want a little funk,” he explains.

From there, Storrie moves on to his everyday high-protein staple: a deconstructed burger. Acknowledging that his ingredient list is so minimal that the producers asked him to chop an onion just to get extra knife footage, Storrie karate-chops a pound of ground beef into portions with his bare hands (“So that I don’t get salmonella comments or whatever, I’m going to wash my hands for you people,” he quips) and cooks the patties in grass-fed butter, before topping it with provolone, arugula, thick slices of beefsteak tomato, and a generous squeeze of Dijon mustard. (Another pro tip: he saves the leftover pan grease to cook his six morning eggs the next day.)

Between flipping patties, Storrie reflects on his style evolution, from growing up in Odessa, Texas (“a lot of long cargo shorts, really messed-up tennis shoes, band tees”) and moving to California during the 2016 drop-crotch jogger era, to sitting front row alongside Madonna and Kate Moss at Saint Laurent. He also addresses the internet’s reaction to his recent buzzcut. "I feel like every six months, I’m a completely different person, and I try to honor that,” he says. ‘I like the hair, but people were pissed off. People were not happy. Whatever, screw it. I’m doing my thing.”

While Now Serving guests typically pull out all the stops to impress the crew, Storrie notes that no one is rushing to sample his ultra-minimalist spread. “I don’t care. I like it,” he says with a shrug, before happily polishing off the plate himself. (His next stop? A workout, of course.)

#6536. The Tucson Restaurant Turning Cactus Into Fine Dining

Traipsing through Tucson Mountain Park, a Midwestern blow-in might not identify much to eat. Plants armed with burs, barbs, and spines all but scream “do not touch.” For chef Aaron Lopez and June Chee, however, this prickly, dusty landscape stocks a pantry of possibility. The married co-owners of Ursa see the Arizona desert as a rich ground for foraging.

Gray, tangled brittlebush, which the average Tucsonan walks or drives by almost daily, can be pressure-cooked, caramelized until black, and baked into cake. Dusty, sage-colored salt bush, when hung to dry, takes on an intensely umami, aquatic saltiness like seaweed. The sweet buds of the Seussian-green palo verde tree become briny, like olives, when suffused with lye.

Don’t even get Lopez started on the dozens of cacti varieties that thrive here, which the restaurant sources from local grower Toadlet Farm and which Lopez harvests throughout the year. The restaurant processes the young and mature paddles, fruit and their seeds, buds, and flowers, which are then grilled, poached, cold-smoked, juiced, dehydrated, nixtamalized, or preserved into jam, wine, and vinegar.

There are hundreds of edible plants in the Sonoran Desert. Ursa strives to showcase their potential, one 10-course meal at a time.

“We treat Ursa as an art showroom, demonstrating to people what these plants can do, what sustainable means, and what was here before it got easy,” says Lopez. The idea was inspired in part by his Sonoran grandfather, Hector Lopez, who died in the spring. “He was the first person I ever heard say they’re proud to be from the desert,” the chef said.

Ursa began as a pop-up in California in 2023. Lopez and Chee moved to a historic brick building in downtown Tucson, re-opening their doors in October 2025. It’s a homecoming of sorts for the couple, who are both from the Sonoran Desert borderlands. They met in Hawaii, where Chee was working in clean energy and transportation. Lopez, meanwhile, spent roughly 18 years cooking in fine dining and modern progressive restaurants like Redbird and Orsa & Winston in LA, and Pai Honolulu. But he was longing for the desert.

After helping a friend open a restaurant and hosting a few popups in Austin, Lopez and Chee bought a desert foraging guide, packed up their two dogs and began driving around the Southwest. It made sense to settle in Tucson, which was recognized by UNESCO in 2015 as a Creative City of Gastronomy for its continuous 4,000-year agricultural history and deeply rooted Sonoran Desert food traditions.

“That’s a unique thing about being here, the connection from seed to plant to restaurant that we hadn’t been able to grasp before,” Chee says.

Consider a recent course that Ursa built around tepary beans, in which the ancient, nutty bean is refried and topped with h:al squash that’s been lactofermented. The squash’s leaves are fermented to make Japanese-style kosho and its flowers are pickled, dried, crushed with dried saltbush, then tossed with barrel cactus seeds for a desert furikake. It’s served with grilled coins of chorizo made from Lopez’s great-grandmother’s recipe and housemade flour tortillas, to all be washed down with an amazake drink made from fermented wheat and goat fat. Don’t get too attached, however. Riffs owing to finicky ingredient availability occur here almost daily.

Running a restaurant using only ingredients foraged and farmed from within about eight to 10 miles means abiding by pretty intense guardrails. The only wheat used is pima club, an ancient soft white variety cultivated for centuries by the Akimel O’odham (Pima) people. Ursa does not use cucumbers, radishes or citrus.

“We’re not trying to substitute anything, like, ‘How do we achieve cucumber? Let’s grab a cactus,’” Lopez says. “We have to throw everything out, really strip it down. Sometimes we have to let the ingredients be bitter or spicy. We have to put our egos aside and let the ingredient be the star.”

For staff who didn’t grow up or learn to cook here, the learning curve at Ursa can feel a little like alighting on a new planet, even if certain flora happen to resemble prickly weeds in their own backyards.

“We have these really cool moments in the restaurant where people are like, Oh! I have lamb’s quarter just growing in my yard!” Chee says of the spinach-like desert green that appears all over Ursa’s menu.

A young Aaron Lopez with his grandfather Hector Lopez.

Ursa’s approach isn’t always easy for customers to understand, so the couple came up with a more down-to-earth option. This fall, the restaurant debuted a four-course, family-style Lineage menu for $75, alongside the existing 10-course Harvest menu ($150). There’s now a pozole course inspired by the family’s annual springtime tradition of roasting goat in agave leaves, barbacoa-style, and shredding it for soup, and a red masa tamal with glazed quail and yucca blossoms in mole made with burnt mesquite bread, a technique Lopez remembers from childhood.

The idea took shape during Ursa’s extended summer break, as Lopez recovered from foot surgery and reflected on the loss of his late grandfather, the tenacious keeper of family traditions.

“I feel so much closer to my ancestors and the land; we want Ursa to be less esoteric and more soulful,” he says. “The story of Ursa is partly of the desert, partly my family. Now we’ve advanced to the point where they’re symbiotic, and I can't tell them apart.”

#6535. The Real-Life Wardrobe of Michael Bennett, Who Traded the NFL for Furniture Design

When you’ve won a Super Bowl ring, made three Pro Bowl appearances, and played a key role on one of the most dominant defensive squads ever—the Seattle Seahawks’ 2010s-era Legion of Boom—what do you do next? For Michael Bennett, the answer was to head back to school.

After completing his 11-year NFL career in 2020, the 41-year-old enrolled at two institutions—the University of Hawaii and Seattle’s Heritage School of Interior Design—to study architecture and interior design, respectively. “I’m a student of whatever I do,” Bennett tells me. “My best quality—and probably my worst quality—is that the things I love to do, I try to become the best. I play tennis five days a week. I’m trying to go to Wimbledon. And design and architecture are like that.”

All that effort is paying off. Through his design practice Studio Kër, Bennett debuted an 11-piece collection of avant-garde furniture inspired by the African diaspora in 2024, which was well received by critics. He’s now hard at work on his sophomore line, alongside a spoken-word album and the occasional bespoke garment.

That last side quest should come as no surprise, because Bennett has some of the most distinctive personal style I’ve ever seen on a pro athlete–current or former—with a particularly clean headwear and accessories game. Here, Bennett tells me all about the skills he carried over from football into his new career, what fatherhood has taught him about masculinity, and the song he listens to every day.

Michael Bennett: I’ve been playing football my whole life, man. After winning so much, I dug deep. I had already conquered the body. How do I conquer the mind? At what point am I being selfish? I’m missing so much of my kids’ lives. I’ve already been to the highest of the high. Am I going to leave my family with a broken man? That was really the question. Am I chasing ego or am I chasing something else? In reality, a lot of us are just chasing the ego, to be remembered, scared of the death of what [your life] was rather than [embracing] the growth that can be.

People want to keep others in a certain box because that’s the way that they understand them. That’s in any relationship. If you started to date somebody when they’re 20 and you turn 40 and they start to change, you’d be like, “You used to like your eggs like that.” People don’t allow others to transition; won’t allow people to actually experience growth. Often you’re meeting people in a time where they’re just starting to learn who they are. Over time you start to really develop who you are.

The truth is it doesn’t matter if people take you seriously, [as long as] you take yourself seriously. What are you doing to practice your craft? Artists are like, “Oh, my practice, my practice.” I never really understood what that meant until I started doing my own practice. I practiced on the field and I can practice the body. But really, if you want to be taken seriously intellectually, then you have to practice the mind. Sometimes practicing the mind is also connected to the body. In football, yeah, you are connected to the mind in a certain way. But it isn’t always like learning to be a lawyer or an architect or an artist—to be a thinker, you’re doing something completely different. And it’s just allowing yourself to transition. Man, truthfully, you got to say fuck everybody.

I think it’s one of the most intellectual sports in general. Tennis is one of those sports where it’s about the angle, the quick twitch. You’re by yourself. With football, it’s the amount of moving parts. People overlook the amount of detail that it takes to run a team—practicing and going through a play 3,000 times before you actually get it. The best players I ever met were the smartest when it came to the sport. They were the PhDs of their craft.

It’s taught me vulnerability. It made me a better human. In some ways, my daughters have allowed me to mature. The sport of football requires so much masculinity. I’m not saying that all masculinity is toxic, [but] it’s more about, how do you hunt but still be gentle? The true samurai doesn’t strike, but knows he can.

What my daughters have allowed me to do is develop my whole humanity. To have a daughter is so special—women are very special. As an athlete, people come back from injuries, but to see a woman come back from giving birth is a whole other level of love. My daughters have been my greatest accomplishments in my life. I never made a Super Bowl trophy. There’s always another winner. But there’s only one Peyton, there’s only one Blake, and there’s one Ollie. As a maker, those are the most special things that I could make.

In 2019, I was really into Booker T. Washington and W.E.B. Du Bois and [their debate over] the “Talented Tenth.” [Booker T. Washington believed that] intellectualism should never get away from the idea of making. I got into design because I’ve always been involved in politics, and politically, I started to realize that everything came down to design.

Shirt and pants by Studio Kër. Shoes by Collegium.

Whenever I spoke out about police brutality or on critical issues in America, that was really where I started to think about design as this language—this form of resistance. How can I change the system? It starts with design. Where I grew up, a non-gentrified area that was low income, it’s like you could see that there was no empathetic way of thinking about design. The definition of architecture for me is empathy for space. That’s what led me to this idea of these African diaspora forms and languages that I will use as my form of resistance.

I’m working on a new collection of furniture. The first collection I did was called “We Gotta Get Back to the Crib,” which to me was really about getting back to the essence of Blackness. A lot of times we talk about Blackness and it’s always connected to traumatic experience. But to me, it was more about how can I connect to these true levels of love, these things really shaped my culture, my family, my mother, my grandmother, and everything that was beautiful about being Black? This next collection is about African brutalism. How can I bring these things that are seen in the ghetto in America and in West Africa and then turn those into ideas about furniture? A lot of times what I’m dealing with as a designer is this idea of abstraction. How can I pull and reference something in such a sweet way? Like how Virgil designed shoes with references, leaving crumbs to this unspoken past. As a designer, that’s what I’m trying to do.

As an athlete, if you talk about your cars or you talk about your jewelry, the way that you gained it doesn’t have that kind of Jay-Z effect—you didn’t hustle to get that. You played to get that, which is different from somebody hustling to get that. With spoken word, I think about Gil Scott-Heron or The Last Poets. They’re talking about critical issues. My perspective is really about humanizing the Black experience and the Black man. My stories and what I’m trying to tell with this music, E-Nigg-Ma, is so much about Black culture, Black design, Black features, this idea of what America is trying to suffocate about Blackness and not let it breathe.

Cuff by Dries van Noten. Ring by Olithica. Watch by Patek Philippe.

Music. When I’m designing, beautiful sounds are really important to the way that I think. My number-one song that I always listen to is Miles Davis’s “Flamenco Sketches.” It’s my daily listen. Those are the sounds that I need to hear: the horn, the riffs, the in-between.

My studio inspires me, just the way light hits. It’s the simplest things. Seeing my family movies. My wife inspires me with what she’s designing.

My great-grandpa, Hall Mack, everybody talked about his fashion. People still talk about his style. He was the first person I saw dry cleaning everything. His style was impeccable. When I look back at a period of style that I liked, it’d be the years of the Birth of the Cool. People like Miles, Sidney Poitier, everybody was just fresh.

I’ve always been connected to style. People always call me “Runway Mike.” They say, “Bro, you wear more Margiela than anybody I know.” I design my own clothes. [Style] is a part of who you are. I love the idea of fashion. I want to design a fashion show. Yo, Wales Bonner, let me design something for you! I want to be backstage.

Over time I just found me. That takes so much time. I feel like one of the most beautiful things is Instagram and this ability to share things, but one of the worst things is Instagram and the ability to share things. Because there’s a part of us that starts to mimic [what we see] in a way that isn’t true to us. We start to judge ourselves on other people’s experience.

It’s cool to see things, but it’s also cool to experiment with what you feel good in. “Yo, this is what I look good in. I don’t care what nobody says, I feel good.” That’s what true fashion is. I buy Prada because I actually like it. That’s the development of who you are and your taste—when you buy things for the love of it. Like, “Man, I really love the shoulder on this.” I’m not buying anything to be seen in it. I’m buying it because I respect the process.

I think it was something from Acne, even though Acne was that middle kind of brand. Acne now has gotten too expensive.

Two things. I bought this striped Prada sweater. It was just a nice, beautiful brown. It was quiet, but it was super nice. And I just designed the blue shirt [from my second look]. Even making something like that is expensive.

I just sketch it, and then I make it in LA.

Yeah, or show a picture of something and break it down like, “Cut this out. I need the arms to be like this.”

I’m also going to do it for my studio. My goal is to have studio attire that I produce. This year I’m dropping four shirts. If you’re a designer and you want a beautiful shirt, here’s four of them. I’m only making a hundred of them. Keep it very simple.

The thing that’s exciting about fashion now is getting away from logos and getting back to beautiful garments. I always loved Issey Miyake, because it’s just so uniform for me. It’s something I wear in the studio all the time—easy to put on, mix and match. It travels well. He was a genius when it came to innovation. A lot of people make clothes, but not a lot of people innovate. I like Wales Bonner. I always like her polo shirts. Margiela and Prada are two of my favorite brands of all time—Prada is just so detailed. Jil Sander is nice. I like Toteme.

Tunnel style is terrible. It’s manufactured. It’s not real. The clothes are wearing them. Half of the things aren’t really who they are. There are some people, like Laremy Tunsil, that are fresh—he’s a big guy from Washington who dresses fresh and it feels like it’s him. But a lot of times you see people that just look like they’re trying too hard to do fashion. Fashion should be quiet and it should be proportioned properly. There’s a geometry to it, and I think that’s what’s missing from tunnel style.

It’s not the sport, it’s the individual. There are some fresh individuals from each sport that wear dope clothes, like Shai Gilgeous-Alexander. Stefon Diggs. My brother Martellus dresses fresh.

Jay-Z’s 4:44. Miles Davis’s Kind of Blue. And I’m in between Kanye West’s Late Registration and Mos Def & Talib Kweli Are Black Star.

#6534. Sugar Plum Thumbprint Cookies

The sugar plums:Here, we’ve used walnuts, prunes, apricots, and dates, but feel free to switch it up as you like! Hazelnuts and dried cherries or pecans, almonds, and raisins would be lovely in the mix. The filling comes together in minutes in a mini food processor, but if you don’t have one, simply chop the mixture as finely as possible. (Use a little oil on your knife to make chopping a little easier.) It’s uncooked, but a little time in the oven gives the spices a chance to warm up and lets the flavor meld. To toast the walnuts, set them on a rimmed baking sheet and bake at 350° until fragrant and golden brown, about 8 minutes.

#6533. The Best Bridal Shops in NYC to Find Your Dream Wedding Dress

From multi-brand salons to designer showrooms, the best bridal shops in NYC are worth making appointments at to find every piece of your wedding wardrobe.

Whether you live in the U.S. or beyond, New York City is the premier destination to shop for a wedding dress. The best bridal shops in NYC run the gamut from singular showrooms for locally based ateliers, flagship stores for international brands, and salons featuring curated selections from a number of top bridal designers. To-be-weds looking for their own wedding wardrobe can always benefit from a trip to multiple bridal shops around New York to help them discover some of the most beautifully made and innovative designs in the bridal industry.

As a New York local who tried over 100 dresses ahead of her own wedding, wore five looks over her wedding weekend, and regularly attends bridal fashion week both in New York and Barcelona, I am constantly asked where to shop in the city. I myself went to 15 different salons over the course of my search for the perfect wardrobe (and had repeat visits at multiple). While I always advise brides to do a little research to understand the styles they like and what brands they are drawn to, I usually give the same advice. First, try out one or two multi-brand salons with styles within your budget that carry designers you are interested in. This can give you an opportunity to try multiple silhouettes and see options from a variety of designers’ perspectives. Then, choose a few individual brand salons and showrooms to visit.

It’s important to take into consideration that many stores require an appointment fee—and that those can book out months in advance. Also, some stores might offer trunk shows showcasing larger, new collections from certain designers seasonally. So you should invest your time and money strategically into the shops that align with your style and will have the selection you are interested in. However, don’t be afraid to try something different—often, brides fall in love with a wedding dress they never expected.

Ready to start your wedding shopping journey? Ahead—and in no particular order—see our selection of the best bridal shops in NYC.

Mark Ingram Bridal Atelier is often the first stop we would recommend for a bride seeking a wedding gown. You can start your journey trying a wide range of silhouettes from legacy luxury designers and up-and-coming fashion-forward brands. Store owner Mark Ingram is a designer himself, and carries his own brand with classic-leaning silhouettes in store. Those looking for a party dress can also find shorter silhouettes in stock at the Midtown bridal salon.

Designers in Stock: Mira Zwillinger, Dana Harel, Elie Saab, Elly Sofocli, Naeem Khan, Lela Rose, Ines Di Santo, Marmar Halim, Valentini, Mark Ingram Bride, and Vera Wang Haute.

Appointment Fee: Complimentary for a standard appointment. Room services are available starting at $450, which include additional guests, extended appointment times, and beverage service.

Alteration Services: In-house alterations available.

For brides with a slightly more bohemian sensibility, give Spina Bride a try. The luxury bridal salon carries chic designers with a dreamier flair that aren’t often found in most major cities. With a mix of avant-garde and more traditional finds, we often advise this Chelsea salon as a must-stop location when taking a trip to NYC for dress shopping. The multi-boutique salon has also recently partnered with bridal brand Lihi Hod, which opened its flagship on the ground floor. Appointments must be made separately to explore the brand’s selection.

Designers in Stock: Lihi Hod, Floure Studio, J. Andreatta, Yellow by Sahar, Ferrah, Francesca Miranda, Santos Costura, Costarellos, A La Robe, and Chana Marelus.

Appointment Fee: $100 fee, which is applied to a purchase.

Alteration Services: Spina recommends two independent tailors for off-site alterations.

Located in Tribeca, Jaxon James has a light-filled space ready for a relaxed, personalized shopping experience. Many designers in this salon have styles that lean towards lace, embellishments, and dramatic silhouettes. A large collection of bridal minis also offers the chance to find flirty party looks.

Designers in Stock: Eden Aharon, Maison Margot, Netta Benshabu, Noy Eliyahu, Pallas Couture Privée, Zuleyha Kuru, House of Savin, Jane Hill, Alyne, Rivini, Mariana Hardwick, and Angel Rivera.

Appointment Fee: $50 for a standard appointment and $100 for exclusive trunk shows. Fee is applied to a purchase.

Alteration Services: Jaxon James recommends independent tailors for off-site alterations.

If you have ever watched Say Yes to the Dress, you are well aware of Kleinfeld. But don’t worry… a visit doesn’t mean your appointment will be seen on TV. The famous bridal salon offers appointments to thousands of brides annually who come for the wide range of designers in their store. Stylists will pull options for you based on intake forms before your appointment, and you can also browse designers currently showcased on the floor. Many plus-size brides choose to start their journey at Kleinfeld as it has the largest selection of designer silhouettes in expanded sizing to try in the city. There is also a Generation Tux store within the space for grooms looking for their ensembles.

Designers in Stock: Reem Acra, Viktor & Rolf, Ines Di Santo, Sareh Nouri, Peter Langner, Tony Ward, Pnina Tornai, Lee Petra Grebenau, Enaura, Jaclyn Whyte, Anne Barge, Rita Vinieris, Alyne, Netta BenShabu, Esé Azénabor, Maison Signore, Nicole + Felicia, Savannah Miller, Idan Cohen, Alon Livné,, Justin Alexander Signature, Pronovias, Nadia Manjarrez, Hayley Paige, and more.

Appointment Fee: $50 for standard appointments Wednesday through Friday, $125 for Saturday appointments, and $75 for Sunday appointments. VIP appointments begin at $250. Fee is applied to a purchase.

Alteration Services: In-house alterations available.

The NYC outpost of Lovely Bride is a favorite as it provides an elevated experience for clients while offering gowns at more accessible price points. The curation is extensive as well, with options for those seeking traditional gowns, minimal silhouettes, vintage-inspired designs, and contemporary creations.

Designers in Stock: Newhite, Katherine Tash, Saint, Dany Tabet, Renhue, Rue De Seine, Moira Hughes, MWL, Vagabond, Louvienne, Alyssa Kristin, Georgia Young, Savannah Miller, Seraphine, Divine Atelier, and La Premiere.

Appointment Fee: $50 for a standard appointment with four guests and $150 for upgraded appointment with six guests. Fee is applied to a purchase.

Alteration Services: Outside alterations required.

Just off Bryant Park is Bridal Reflections, a massive family-owned bridal salon. Those looking for the embellished styles of Kim Kassas, classic Pronovias silhouettes, and tons of selections from high-end designers can find them at this popular boutique.

Designers in Stock: Leah Da Gloria, Kim Kassas Couture, Adi Shlomo, Galia Lahav, Eve of Milady, Milla Nova, Enzoani, Lazaro, Maison Perez by Lazaro, Michael DePaulo, Pronovias, Maggie Sottero, Amalia Carrara by Eve of Milady, Shiran Abergel, Adam Zohar, Stephen Yearick, and Ysa Makino.

Appointment Fee: $100 for a standard appointment and $750 for a three-hour VIP appointment. Fee is applied to a purchase.

Alteration Services: In-house alterations available.

Does your style lean more eclectic? Then you’ll want to take a look at the selection of bridal looks at Belle Atelier. The salon offers dresses for those who want their wedding wardrobe to make a sartorial statement. In-house alterations are also a key part of the atelier’s ethos, and the salon even offers the ability to collaborate on custom designs.

Designers in Stock: Vivienne Westwood, Varca, Wed Studio, Bretagne, Di Petsa, Richard Quinn, and Prea James.

Appointment Fee: $25 for a mini appointment (1-2 dresses), $50 for a one-hour appointment, $120 for a two-hour appointment, and $35 for an accessories appointment.

Alteration Services: In-house alterations available.

Visiting Bergdorf Goodman is already a treat—but going to find your wedding dress is extra special. The department store carries a great selection of gowns and accessories from luxury bridal designers in its private bridal salon. Best of all, you can easily start on your shoe search afterwards a few floors below.

Designers in Stock: Andrew Kwon, Amsale, CD Greene, Cucculelli Shaheen, Elie Saab, Enaura, Giambattista Valli, Homa Bridal, Ines Di Santo, Jaclyn Whyte, Monvieve, Naeem Khan, Reem Acra, Sareh Nouri, The Danes New York, Vera Wang, Verdin Bridal, and Viktor & Rolf.

Alteration Services: In-house alterations available.

Although based in Brooklyn, The One Bridal is worth the subway ride. Some of our favorite designers from around the globe have this salon as their only stockist in the five boroughs. Come try on the designs, then spend the rest of your afternoon exploring Industry City.

Designers in Stock: Cortana, Flora, Halfpenny London, Lola Varma, Prea James, Sophie et Voilà, and The Law Bridal.

Appointment Fee: $40 fee which is applied to a purchase.

Alteration Services: In-house alterations available.

Danielle Frankel’s stunning new flagship in Tribeca cements the brand’s presence as the must-visit bridal destination in the city. Located in a converted Mercantile Exchange building, the multi-story salon is not only an aesthetic treat—interior designer Augusta Hoffman curated the space—but also houses Frankel’s fashion-forward gowns, accessories, and large fitting rooms for to-be-weds and their guests to try on garments.

Appointment Fee: $150 fee, which is applied to a purchase.

Alteration Services: In-house alterations available.

On the second floor of Oscar De La Renta’s Madison Avenue store, you’ll find the brand’s flagship bridal salon. From glamorous gowns to fun minis, brides can shop for their entire wedding wardrobe in this luxe space. Make sure to check out downstairs as well for colorful options for yourself and VIPs in your wedding party.

Alteration Services: The brand partners with outside alterations specialists.

Monique Lhuillier’s Upper East Side store is an essential stop on many brides-to-be’s shopping trips. Known for beautiful lace gowns and classic silhouettes, this bright and airy store offers a one-on-one styling session to help guide you towards your dream dress.

Appointment Fee: Complimentary. Appointment fee will be implemented in 2027.

Alteration Services: In-house alterations available.

No name is as synonymous with bridal fashion as Vera Wang. If you want to try on the largest selection of the brand’s haute couture collections, head to its Upper East Side salon, where you can shop new collections and iconic styles from years past in the minimalist boutique.

Alteration Services: In-house alterations available.

Amsale has a light-filled flagship in SoHo that’s perfect for brides hoping to find a dress that fits a modern-meets-classic aesthetic. The salon offers a serene experience as you try your way through their refined silhouettes. The two-story boutique also has ready-to-wear styles perfect for guests, bridesmaids, and mothers of the bride and groom.

Dress Price Starting Point: $1995 for Nouvelle Amsale and $4000 for Amsale.

Appointment Fee: $50 hold fee that is refunded after appointment.

Alteration Services: In-house alterations available.

The stylish interiors of Alexandra Grecco’s NYC flagship salon set the stage for a joyful shopping experience. The SoHo salon not only has the brand’s core silhouettes, but also a few flagship exclusives and runway accessories perfect for the bride looking to push the boundary with their wedding weekend style.

Appointment Fee: $125 for bridal appointment and $50 for accessories-only appointment. Fee is applied to a purchase.

Alteration Services: Outside alterations required.

The moody interiors on Spring Street immediately draw you into the world of Cinq. The vintage-inspired gowns line the walls of this large showroom space, which offers individual appointments for brides to explore the salon with a dedicated stylist.

Appointment Fee: $150 fee, which is applied to a purchase.

Alteration Services: Outside alterations required.

If you want a truly original look for your wedding weekend, consider One/Of. Patricia Voto welcomes you into her jewel-box Upper East Side studio to craft a bespoke piece with original patterns, sourced designer and vintage deadstock fabric, and silhouettes chosen for your exact measurements. Understandably, this labor-intensive creative process raises the price tag, but it’s worth it for a fully custom piece.

Dress Price Starting Point: $16,000 for bespoke looks and $30,000 for bespoke wedding gowns

Appointment Fee: $500 fee which is applied to a purchase.

Alteration Services: In-house alterations available.

Wiederhoeft has become a favorite for couples seeking bold looks with intricate beading and artfully cinched waistlines. With the designer’s corsetry program that allows to-be-weds to perfectly fit their proportions based on bust and torso length, you can ensure the perfect fit as you head down the aisle or dance into the night. An appointment at the Garment District showroom starts with a corset fitting—and ends with you trying tons of fun runway looks.

Appointment Fee: $100 fee, which is applied to a purchase.

Alteration Services: Outside alterations required.

The New York flagship for Australian bridal brand Kyha is the bridal destination of NoHo. While clean, crafted silhouettes are the designer’s bread and butter, each season also brings about trend-forward styles for the bride looking to have some fun with their bridal style. Expect to celebrate with some Champagne as you shop your way through their selection.

Appointment Fee: $50 for accessories styling appointments, $60 for weekday appointments, and $100 for weekend appointments.

Alteration Services: In-house alterations available.

If you love Galia Lahav’s signature lace gowns, the NYC flagship on Wooster Street is a must-visit. The bridal salon features a huge selection of the brand’s dresses from both their Galia and Couture lines, offering a wide range of styles to fit your aesthetic. Helpful stylists will guide you through the collections and offer treats for you and your party as you get laced into the designer’s many corseted styles.

Appointment Fee: $50 to $100 based on day of the week. Fee is applied to a purchase.

Alteration Services: In-house alterations available.

NYC-based designer Sarah Seven has both her namesake line and luxury Sept collection housed in the same building on Lafayette Street. With specialized salons on separate floors, brides can book appointments to explore which styles might fit into their wedding wardrobes.

Dress Price Starting Point: $4,500 for Sarah Seven and $12,000 for Sept

Appointment Fee: $100 fee which is applied to a purchase.

Alteration Services: Outside alterations required.

Milla Nova’s modern showroom is a new destination for brides-to-be downtown. The Ukrainian brand created a warm, minimal space to welcome clients to explore their collections and find their dream gown.

Appointment Fee: $60 for weekday appointments, $100 for weekend appointments, and $700 for private suite appointments. Fee is applied to a purchase.

Alteration Services: In-house alterations available.

Just off of Washington Square Park is Lee Petra Grebenau’s flagship salon. Here, you’ll find the designer’s beautiful lace gowns, fun embellished minis, and a select number of made-to-order styles perfect for reception looks. Stylists guide you through the selections, while providing insights into fit, customizations, and more.

Appointment Fee: $100 fee which is applied to a purchase.

Alteration Services: In-house alterations available.

The bridal collections of Elie Saab are known for their meticulous construction and inventive takes on classic silhouettes. Luckily, the designer’s Madison Avenue store serves as a flagship for the bridal brand. To-be-weds can work with their experienced team to guide them through styling and alterations of their gorgeous gowns.

Alteration Services: In-house alterations available.

With its beautiful corsetry and boundary-pushing aesthetics, Vivienne Westwood has become one of the most popular choices for stylish brides for a reason. The brand recently expanded the footprint of its bridal collection to take over the entire second floor of its NYC flagship, where to-be-weds can try a large selection of gowns from recent made-to-measure and couture collections.

Alteration Services: Outside alterations required.

Anne Barge has transformed a chic Upper East Side apartment into their flagship store. With both their Blue Willow and Anne Barge lines available, as well as their shoe and accessory collections, brides can fully outfit themselves for the walk down the aisle.

Dress Price Starting Point: $2,850 for the Blue Willow collection and $3,700 for the Anne Barge collection

Appointment Fee: $50 for weekday appointments and $100 for weekend appointments. Fee is applied to a purchase.

Alteration Services: In-house alterations available.

Within the Garment District, you’ll find Enaura’s tastefully decorated bridal salon. Adjoining the brand’s atelier, the showroom allows you to have an individualized appointment with a stylist to try on a wide selection of looks from past seasons. Designer Sohil Mistry is also often on hand to discuss construction and speak to customizations.

Appointment Fee: $125 fee, which is applied to a purchase.

Alteration Services: The brand partners with outside alterations specialists.

Lein is a NYC-based favorite to find polished pieces to fit every part of your wedding wardrobe journey. Designer Meredith Stoecklein’s SoHo showroom offers a personalized environment to engage with the brand and try styles from both the bridal and ready-to-wear collections. Lein also works on bespoke projects for clients looking to create something original.

Dress Price Starting Point: $1,500 for civil ceremony, $4000 for gowns, and bespoke pricing upon request.

Appointment Fee: $150 for standard appointments and $250 for bespoke. Fee is applied to purchases.

Alteration Services: In-house alterations available.

Brides who love a slinky slip or two-piece set should make an appointment at Elizabeth Fillmore’s Meatpacking District salon. Adjoining the designer’s HQ, the showroom allows to-be-weds to shop styles old and new from the chic collections.

Appointment Fee: $100 fee which is applied to a purchase.

Alteration Services: In-house alterations available.

If you want to bring a vintage flair to your wedding attire without having to search for an archival piece, check out the collections of Tanner Fletcher. The brand has crafted a gender-inclusive bridal line that mixes beautiful technique with nostalgia and a sense of whimsy. While you can shop pieces that have made their way down the runways, the designers are always open to crafting custom creations for your big day.

Alteration Services: Outside alterations required.

NYC-based brand Markarian has an intimate showroom in the Union Square neighborhood filled with its artfully designed pieces by recent Vogue bride Alexandra O’Neill. While you can find Markarian’s beautiful ready-to-wear styles in stock, the bridal pieces are worth visiting for on their own. If you’re looking to fill out your entire bridal wardrobe, Markarian has thoughtful pieces for more casual events as well as your walk down the aisle.

Appointment Fee: $150 fee, which is applied to a purchase.

Alteration Services: Salon recommends an outside alterations specialist.

Those drawn to Honor’s eclectic, feminine designs should pay a visit to the designer’s newly decorated SoHo salon. As the home base for the brand, you can find the largest selection of styles within these dusty pink interiors. Honor also offers bespoke experiences for brides looking for a special piece from creative director Giovanna Randall.

Appointment Fee: $215 fee, which is applied to a purchase.

Alteration Services: In-house alterations available.

Andrew Kwon offers a white-glove shopping experience in the heart of NYC’s Garment District. Private showroom appointments allow you to be the only client in the room as you explore Kwon’s beautiful designs. If you’re interested in looks in shades other than white for yourself, a bridesmaid, or mother-of-the-bride, the designer’s evening collections are also on display in the showroom.

Appointment Fee: $150 fee, which is applied to a purchase.

Alteration Services: In-house alterations available.

When trying on wedding gowns, it’s important to be prepared so you can have the best overall experience. It’s advised to wear nude undergarments that won’t show through more sheer styles and consider bringing a heel you might like to wear with a gown. You should also avoid wearing heavy makeup and fragrances to appointments. Sample gowns are reworn by many to-be-weds, and many stores ask you to go fresh-faced to avoid makeup transfer. While you can bring a few guests along like a bridesmaid, mom, or stylist, check with each salon’s policies on how big of a party you can bring.

As most wedding dresses take six to eight months to make, it is advised to book your appointments about nine months to a year ahead of your wedding. On rare occasions, you can find designers who might be able to work on shorter timelines. Certain popular designers can book out their appointments months in advance, so as soon as you know you want to start the shopping process, take a look at availability.

#6532. Timothée Chalamet Declares the Official Start of Puffer Season

Like any true New Yorker, Timothée Chalamet has built himself a deep bench of cold-weather staples. We’re talking puffers on puffers on puffers—hailing from The North Face, Supreme, Thug Club and beyond—paired with all manner of boots, including Visvim lace-ups, Red Wing moc toes, and multiple pairs of Timbs (of both the OG Wheat and custom Chrome Hearts varieties.) For all his fashion-guy flourishes, Chalamet’s winter outfits generally have the chops to handle a brick New York sidewalk come February. So yesterday, even though it was still a balmy 68 degrees in NYC, it was no surprise to see Chalamet cheering on his beloved Knicks at Madison Square Garden in yet another excellent down-filled jacket and blizzard-ready boots.

Sitting courtside, the Dune star wore a combination familiar to just about anyone who’s endured winter on the East Coast. The jacket was a dusty pink number from Goldwin, the cult Japanese outdoors brand founded back in 1950. It cuts a sharp silhouette despite packing some serious down insulation, and the windproof, water-resistant nylon is designed to ward off rain, sleet, and snow. The muted exterior has a subtle sheen—not quite Cam’ron pink, but certainly not your average black puffer. Over the past couple years, pink has become one of Chalamet’s signature colors: Last January, he paired a bubblegum Telfar puffer with an Arc’teryx toque and a Chanel purse like it was no big deal; less than a month later, he popped up at the Berlin Film Festival in head-to-toe pastel Chrome Hearts. This time out, he left the handbag at home but topped things off with a Knicks championship hat.

And then there were the boots. At first glance, they could pass for a pair of Uggs, thanks to the familiar shape and cozy suede uppers. (It wouldn’t have been the first time he wore a pair of the Aussie surfer classics courtside.) But these pull-ons were, in fact, from menswear favorite Merrell, built for some truly cold and ugly weather. The outer suede is water-resistant, the lining is insulated, and the rubber outsoles boast some serious traction. Plus, the very gorp-y utility cord at the heel lets you cinch them extra tight. Like the advanced-level dresser he is, Chalamet tucked his baggy black pants into the boots, making sure his footwear got a chance to really shine.

Once again, Chalamet has turned practical winter clothes into an A-list look. While a pink puffer might not be every guy’s idea of cold-weather dressing, there’s something to be said for a winter coat with a little personality. Was celebrity row’s resident heartthrob a few weeks early with this ensemble? Sure, but when that first serious snowfall hits, he’ll be extra ready.
